origin: Greek: hydro (water) and genes (generate)
h: Hydrogen makes up about three-quarters of the ordinary matter in the universe by mass, and it fuels every shining star.
f: Henry Cavendish identified it in 1766; Lavoisier named it 'water-former' because it burns to make water.
It is the lightest gas, and free hydrogen slowly leaks from Earth's upper atmosphere into space.
Most hydrogen today is made from natural gas and used to produce ammonia for fertilizer.
The 1937 Hindenburg disaster ended the era of hydrogen-filled passenger airships.
from: Almost all hydrogen nuclei date from the Big Bang, and hydrogen still makes up about three quarters of ordinary matter by mass.
Stars burn hydrogen into helium for most of their lives, slowly using up the cosmic supply.
On Earth it is mostly bound in water and in hydrocarbons such as natural gas, and free hydrogen gas is rare.
Most industrial hydrogen comes from steam reforming of natural gas, with a small but growing share from electrolysis of water.
uses: Making ammonia for fertilizer through the Haber-Bosch process is the largest use of hydrogen.
Oil refineries use hydrogen to strip sulfur from fuels and to crack heavy oils into lighter products.
Liquid hydrogen burned with liquid oxygen powers many rocket engines and upper stages.
Fuel cells combine hydrogen with oxygen to make electricity for some cars, buses, forklifts and backup generators.
Historical: hydrogen lifted passenger airships until the Hindenburg fire of 1937 ended that era.

who: Sir William Ramsay, Nils Langlet, P. T. Cleve
origin: Greek: hêlios (sun).
h: Helium was discovered in the Sun's spectrum in 1868, decades before anyone found it on Earth.
f: Earth's helium builds up underground from radioactive decay of uranium and thorium, and is extracted from natural gas.
Liquid helium boils at about 4 kelvin and cools the superconducting magnets in MRI scanners.
It is the only element that will not freeze at normal pressure, however cold it gets.
Below about 2.2 kelvin, liquid helium becomes a superfluid that can creep up and over container walls.
from: Most helium formed in the first minutes after the Big Bang, and stars add more by fusing hydrogen in their cores.
On Earth, helium comes from alpha decay of uranium and thorium in rocks and collects in some natural gas reservoirs.
Helium in the air is scarce because the light gas slowly escapes into space.
It is separated from natural gas by cryogenic distillation, with the United States and Qatar the leading producers.
uses: Liquid helium cools the superconducting magnets in MRI scanners and many research instruments.
Chipmakers and optical fiber producers use helium as an inert, heat-conducting atmosphere.
Helium purges and pressurizes rocket fuel tanks and helps detect tiny leaks in vacuum systems.
Deep-sea divers breathe helium-oxygen mixtures to avoid nitrogen narcosis.
Balloons and blimps use helium for lift because it is light and does not burn.

origin: Greek: lithos (stone).
h: Lithium is the lightest metal, so light that it floats on water while fizzing as it reacts.
f: Rechargeable lithium-ion batteries power phones, laptops and electric cars.
Lithium salts have been used since 1949 to treat bipolar disorder.
Much of it comes from salty brines evaporated in vast ponds in the high deserts of South America.
Small amounts of lithium were forged in the Big Bang, along with hydrogen and helium.
from: A little lithium-7 formed in the Big Bang, and cosmic rays striking interstellar gas add more, while stars mostly destroy it.
It is found in brines beneath Andean salt flats and in hard-rock minerals such as spodumene.
Australia mines the most lithium, followed by Chile and China, and China refines most of the world's supply.
Brines are concentrated by evaporation, while the metal itself is made by electrolysis of molten lithium chloride.
uses: Lithium-ion batteries in phones, laptops and electric vehicles are now by far the largest use.
Lithium compounds lower melting temperatures in glass and ceramics, including heat-resistant cookware.
Lithium greases keep machinery lubricated over a wide range of temperatures.
Lithium carbonate is a long-standing treatment for bipolar disorder.
Aluminum-lithium alloys make aircraft structures lighter.

origin: Greek: beryllos, "beryl" (a mineral).
h: Beryllium is almost transparent to X-rays, so it is used for the windows of X-ray tubes and detectors.
f: Emeralds and aquamarines are both forms of beryl, a beryllium aluminum silicate mineral.
Light, stiff and stable in the cold, gold-coated beryllium forms the mirrors of the James Webb Space Telescope.
Its compounds taste sweet, which earned it the early name glucinium; tasting them is a very bad idea.
Inhaling beryllium dust can cause chronic beryllium disease, a serious lung condition.
from: Beryllium is not made in stellar fusion; it forms when cosmic rays shatter carbon, nitrogen and oxygen nuclei in space.
It is rare in Earth's crust and is mined mainly from the minerals bertrandite and beryl.
The United States produces most of the world's beryllium, largely from a mine in Utah.
Ore is converted to beryllium fluoride, which is reduced with magnesium to give the metal.
uses: Copper-beryllium alloys make strong, conductive springs and connectors and spark-free tools for explosive environments.
Its lightness and stiffness suit space optics; the James Webb Space Telescope mirrors are gold-coated beryllium.
Thin beryllium windows let X-rays pass through in medical and scientific equipment.
Beryllium reflects neutrons in some research reactors and nuclear weapons.
Beryllium oxide ceramics carry heat away from high-power electronics while insulating electrically.

who: Sir H. Davy, J. L. Gay-Lussac, L. J. Thénard
origin: From Arabic and Persian words for borax.
h: Boron is the secret of borosilicate glass, such as Pyrex, which survives sudden heating and cooling without cracking.
f: Boron carbide is one of the hardest materials known and is used in body armor.
Boron absorbs neutrons readily, so it is used in nuclear reactor control rods and shielding.
Plants need traces of boron to build healthy cell walls.
In the 1880s, famous twenty-mule teams hauled borax, a boron mineral, out of Death Valley.
from: Like lithium and beryllium, most boron is made by cosmic-ray spallation rather than inside stars.
It concentrates in dry-lake evaporite deposits as borate minerals such as borax, kernite, colemanite and ulexite.
Turkey holds the largest reserves and leads production, followed by the United States.
Borates are mined and refined directly, while pure elemental boron is hard to make and seldom needed.
uses: Borosilicate glass, fiberglass insulation and glass fiber reinforcement use a large share of mined boron.
Boron is an essential plant micronutrient, so borates are added to fertilizers.
Neodymium-iron-boron magnets, the strongest permanent magnets, power motors, wind turbines and headphones.
Boron carbide is extremely hard and serves in body armor, while boron-10 absorbs neutrons in reactor control rods.
Tiny amounts of boron dope silicon to make p-type semiconductors.

origin: Latin: carbo, (charcoal).
h: Carbon's knack for forming endless chains and rings makes it the backbone of every known living thing.
f: Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon; only the arrangement of their atoms differs.
Nearly all the carbon in your body was forged inside stars that died before the Sun was born.
Radiocarbon dating uses carbon-14, with a half-life of about 5,700 years, to date once-living material.
Diamond is the hardest natural material, which is why it tips drills and saws.
from: Carbon is forged in red giant stars by the triple-alpha process, which fuses three helium nuclei.
Stellar winds and planetary nebulae spread it into space, where it joins new stars, planets and organic molecules.
On Earth it occurs in limestone and other carbonates, coal, oil, natural gas, graphite, diamond and all living things.
Coal and graphite are mined, diamonds come from kimberlite pipes, and both graphite and diamond are also made synthetically.
uses: Fossil fuels made of carbon compounds supply most of the world's energy, releasing carbon dioxide when burned.
Coke reduces iron ore in blast furnaces, and a small amount of carbon turns iron into steel.
Graphite forms lithium-ion battery anodes, pencil cores and electrodes for electric arc furnaces.
Activated carbon filters water and air, and carbon fiber makes light, stiff aircraft parts and sports gear.
Radiocarbon dating with carbon-14 measures the age of organic remains up to about 50,000 years old.

origin: Greek: nitron and genes, (soda forming).
h: Nitrogen makes up about 78 percent of the air you breathe, yet most living things cannot use it directly.
f: The Haber–Bosch process turns air's nitrogen into ammonia, making the fertilizer that feeds billions of people.
Liquid nitrogen boils at minus 196 °C and is used to freeze biological samples and food.
Nitrogen is part of every protein and every strand of DNA.
Lightning and certain soil bacteria naturally convert nitrogen into forms plants can absorb.
from: Nitrogen is made mainly by the CNO cycle, which fuses hydrogen into helium in stars heavier than the Sun.
It makes up about 78 percent of Earth's atmosphere and is found in nitrate minerals and all proteins.
Pure nitrogen is separated from air by cryogenic distillation, or by membranes and pressure-swing adsorption.
uses: Ammonia made from nitrogen and hydrogen is the basis of most nitrogen fertilizer.
Nitrogen gas blankets packaged food, chemical tanks and electronics factories to keep oxygen out.
Liquid nitrogen flash-freezes food and preserves cells, embryos and other biological samples.
Nitrogen compounds are building blocks for explosives, nylon, dyes and many medicines.
Historical: Chilean saltpeter was the main nitrate source for fertilizer and explosives before the Haber-Bosch process.

origin: Greek: oxys and genes, (acid former).
h: Oxygen is the most abundant element in Earth's crust by mass, mostly locked up in rocks as silicates and oxides.
f: The oxygen in our air was released by photosynthesis, starting with ancient bacteria over two billion years ago.
Liquid oxygen is pale blue and is attracted to a magnet.
Ozone, a three-atom form of oxygen high in the atmosphere, shields the surface from much harmful ultraviolet light.
Scheele and Priestley each isolated it in the 1770s, and Lavoisier gave it its name.
from: Oxygen forms in massive stars by helium capture on carbon, and supernovae scatter it widely.
It is the most abundant element in Earth's crust, bound in silicates, oxides and water.
Photosynthesis by plants and microbes produced the free oxygen that makes up about 21 percent of air.
Industrial oxygen is separated from liquefied air by fractional distillation.
uses: Steelmaking blows pure oxygen through molten iron to burn off excess carbon, the largest single use.
Hospitals give medical oxygen to patients with breathing difficulties.
Oxyacetylene torches use oxygen to cut and weld metal.
Liquid oxygen is the oxidizer for many rocket engines.
Oxygen helps treat wastewater and is a feedstock for chemicals such as ethylene oxide.

origin: Latin: fluere (flow).
h: Fluorine is the most reactive element of all, combining with almost everything, even the supposedly inert gas xenon.
f: Fluoride in toothpaste and drinking water strengthens tooth enamel against decay.
Attempts to isolate it injured several chemists; Henri Moissan finally succeeded in 1886 and later won a Nobel Prize.
Teflon's slippery nonstick coating is a chain of carbon atoms sheathed in fluorine.
Its mineral fluorite gave us the word 'fluorescence', because some samples glow under ultraviolet light.
from: Fluorine is cosmically scarce because fusion easily destroys it; it is thought to be made mainly in aging giant stars.
Its main mineral is fluorite, calcium fluoride, and China is the leading producer.
Phosphate rock also contains fluorine, which is recovered during fertilizer production.
Henri Moissan first isolated it in 1886 by electrolysis, still the method used today.
uses: Hydrofluoric acid made from fluorite is the starting point for refrigerants and nonstick PTFE coatings.
Uranium hexafluoride gas makes it possible to enrich uranium for nuclear fuel.
Fluoride in toothpaste and drinking water helps prevent tooth decay.
Many medicines and pesticides contain fluorine atoms that make them more stable in the body or environment.
Lithium-ion battery electrolytes and binders rely on fluorine compounds.

who: Sir William Ramsay, M. W. Travers
origin: Greek: neos (new).
h: Neon glows a vivid reddish-orange when electricity passes through it, the classic color of neon signs.
f: Many other 'neon' sign colors actually come from different gases or from coatings inside the tubes.
William Ramsay and Morris Travers discovered it in 1898; its name comes from the Greek for 'new'.
It is extracted from liquefied air, where it makes up only about 18 parts per million.
Neon is so unreactive that it forms no stable chemical compounds.
from: Neon forms in massive stars by carbon burning and is released in supernovae, making it common in the cosmos.
Earth's atmosphere holds only about 18 parts per million of neon.
It is collected as a byproduct of large air separation plants that produce oxygen and nitrogen.
uses: Excimer lasers used to pattern computer chips use neon as their main buffer gas.
Neon signs glow red-orange when electricity passes through the gas.
Helium-neon lasers serve in labs and alignment tools, and once read barcodes at checkouts.
Liquid neon is a compact refrigerant for cryogenic equipment.

origin: Medieval Latin: sodanum, (headache remedy); symbol from Latin natrium, (sodium carbonate).
h: Sodium is a soft metal that reacts violently with water, yet combined with chlorine it becomes ordinary table salt.
f: It is soft enough to cut with a knife, revealing a shiny surface that tarnishes within moments.
Your nerve cells fire signals by moving sodium and potassium ions across their membranes.
Sodium-vapor streetlamps produce a distinctive, intense yellow-orange glow.
Humphry Davy first isolated it in 1807 by passing electricity through molten caustic soda.
from: Sodium is made by carbon burning in massive stars and released in supernovae.
It is the sixth most abundant element in Earth's crust and the main metal dissolved in seawater.
Rock salt is mined and sea salt is evaporated from seawater, while soda ash comes from trona deposits.
Metallic sodium is made by electrolysis of molten sodium chloride.
uses: Sodium chloride seasons and preserves food, de-ices roads and is the raw material for chlorine and caustic soda.
Sodium hydroxide and sodium carbonate are used to make paper, soap, glass and many chemicals.
Low-pressure sodium vapor lamps give some streetlights their yellow-orange glow.
Liquid sodium cools some fast nuclear reactors.
Sodium-ion batteries are emerging as a cheaper alternative to lithium-ion for stationary storage.

origin: From Magnesia ancient city in district of Thessaly, Greece.
h: Magnesium burns with a dazzling white light, once used for photographic flashes and still used in flares and fireworks.
f: A magnesium atom sits at the heart of every chlorophyll molecule, helping plants capture sunlight.
It is the lightest metal commonly used for structures, found in alloys for cars, laptops and aircraft.
It is produced from minerals such as dolomite and from magnesium salts in seawater and brines.
Epsom salt is magnesium sulfate, named after a mineral spring in Epsom, England.
from: Magnesium forms in massive stars by carbon and neon burning and is spread by supernovae.
It is abundant in Earth's mantle and crust, in minerals such as dolomite and magnesite, and dissolved in seawater.
China produces most magnesium metal, mainly by the Pidgeon process, which reduces roasted dolomite with ferrosilicon.
Electrolysis of molten magnesium chloride from brines or seawater is the other main route.
uses: Alloying aluminum for beverage cans and car parts is the largest use of magnesium.
Magnesium alloys make light car parts, laptop cases and power tool housings.
It removes sulfur from molten iron and reduces titanium and zirconium compounds to metal.
Magnesium oxide lines furnaces, and magnesium compounds are used in antacids and laxatives.
Flares and fireworks use burning magnesium for brilliant white light.

origin: Latin: alumen, aluminis, (alum).
h: Before cheap smelting arrived in 1886, aluminum was a precious metal, prized enough to cap the Washington Monument.
f: It is the most abundant metal in Earth's crust, but almost never occurs naturally as pure metal.
The Hall–Héroult process, invented independently by two young chemists in 1886, extracts it using huge amounts of electricity.
A thin oxide skin forms instantly on its surface, protecting it from further corrosion.
Recycling aluminum uses only about 5 percent of the energy needed to make it from ore.
from: Aluminum forms in massive stars during carbon and neon burning, and radioactive aluminum-26 traces recent star formation.
It is the most abundant metal in Earth's crust, but it is extracted mostly from bauxite.
Australia, Guinea and China lead bauxite mining, and China makes more than half of the world's aluminum.
The Bayer process refines bauxite to alumina, which the Hall-Héroult process electrolyzes into metal.
uses: Cars, trucks, aircraft and trains use aluminum to save weight.
Beverage cans, foil and food packaging are made from aluminum and are widely recycled.
Window frames, siding and curtain walls use aluminum for its corrosion resistance.
Overhead power lines use aluminum conductors because they are light and inexpensive.
Historical: before cheap electrolysis in 1886, aluminum was costlier than silver and showcased like a precious metal.

origin: Latin: silex, silicus, (flint).
h: Silicon is the heart of modern electronics: nearly every computer chip is built on an ultra-pure silicon wafer.
f: It is the second most abundant element in Earth's crust, mostly locked in sand and silicate rocks.
Silicon solar cells generate most of the world's solar electricity.
Silicones, used in sealants and bakeware, are flexible polymers built on a silicon–oxygen backbone.
Jöns Jacob Berzelius is usually credited with isolating it in 1824.
from: Silicon is made by oxygen burning in massive stars and released by supernovae.
It is the second most abundant element in Earth's crust, forming quartz and silicate minerals.
Quartz is reduced with carbon in electric arc furnaces, and China produces most of the world's silicon.
Electronic-grade silicon is purified chemically and grown into large single crystals by the Czochralski method.
uses: Silicon is alloyed with aluminum for castings and with iron as ferrosilicon for steelmaking.
Ultrapure silicon wafers are the basis of computer chips and most solar panels.
Silicones, polymers with silicon-oxygen backbones, make sealants, lubricants, cookware and medical devices.
Silica sand is the main ingredient of glass and an essential component of concrete.

origin: Greek: phosphoros, (bringer of light).
h: Phosphorus was discovered in 1669 by Hennig Brand, who boiled down huge quantities of urine searching for the philosopher's stone.
f: White phosphorus glows faintly in the dark as it slowly reacts with oxygen in the air.
Phosphate groups form the backbone of DNA and carry energy in the molecule ATP.
Your bones and teeth are built largely from calcium phosphate minerals.
Most mined phosphate rock ends up as fertilizer for crops.
from: Phosphorus is produced in massive stars during neon and oxygen burning and released by supernovae.
Its main source is phosphate rock; Morocco holds most known reserves, and China is the largest producer.
Phosphate rock is treated with sulfuric acid to make phosphoric acid, or heated with coke and silica to free the element.
Hennig Brand first isolated it in 1669 from boiled-down urine.
uses: Most mined phosphate becomes fertilizer, since plants cannot grow without phosphorus.
Phosphoric acid and phosphates are food additives, flavoring cola drinks and leavening baking powder.
Red phosphorus coats the striking surface of safety matchboxes.
Lithium iron phosphate is a common cathode in batteries for electric vehicles and grid storage.
Historical: phosphates softened water in laundry detergents until algae blooms led many places to restrict them.

origin: Latin: sulfur (brimstone).
h: Sulfur, the 'brimstone' of old, forms bright yellow crystals around volcanic vents and hot springs.
f: Sulfur compounds are behind the smells of rotten eggs, skunk spray and garlic.
Sulfuric acid is made in larger quantities than almost any other industrial chemical.
Charles Goodyear's vulcanization process uses sulfur to turn sticky natural rubber into tough, elastic rubber.
Sulfur burns with a blue flame, giving off choking sulfur dioxide gas.
from: Sulfur forms in massive stars by oxygen burning and is scattered by supernovae.
It occurs as native sulfur near volcanoes and in salt domes, and in sulfide and sulfate minerals.
Most sulfur now comes from removing hydrogen sulfide from natural gas and crude oil.
Historical: the Frasch process melted underground sulfur with superheated water and pumped it to the surface.
uses: Most sulfur is turned into sulfuric acid, one of the most produced industrial chemicals.
Sulfuric acid makes phosphate fertilizers, leaches copper ores and fills lead-acid batteries.
Vulcanization with sulfur makes rubber tires tough and elastic.
Sulfur is a fungicide for crops and an ingredient of gunpowder.
Sulfites preserve wine and dried fruit.

origin: Greek: chlôros (greenish yellow).
h: Chlorine gas was a deadly weapon in World War I, yet chlorine disinfection now keeps much of the world's drinking water safe.
f: It is a yellow-green gas, and its name comes from the Greek for 'pale green'.
Carl Scheele made it in 1774, but Humphry Davy showed it was an element in 1810.
It is made by passing electricity through salty water, which also yields sodium hydroxide.
PVC plastic, used for pipes and window frames, is more than half chlorine by mass.
from: Chlorine forms in massive stars during oxygen burning and is released in supernovae.
On Earth it is found almost entirely as chloride, in seawater, salt lakes and rock salt deposits.
Chlorine gas is made by electrolysis of brine in the chlor-alkali process, which also yields sodium hydroxide.
uses: Making PVC plastic is the largest single use of chlorine.
Chlorine and its compounds disinfect drinking water and swimming pools.
Sodium hypochlorite solution is household bleach.
Chlorine is an intermediate in making many solvents, medicines and titanium dioxide pigment.
Historical: chlorine gas was used as a chemical weapon in World War I.

origin: Greek: argos (inactive).
h: Argon is the third most abundant gas in Earth's air, at almost 1 percent, far more than carbon dioxide.
f: Its name comes from the Greek for 'lazy', because it reacts with almost nothing.
Rayleigh and Ramsay discovered it in 1894 after noticing that nitrogen taken from air was oddly heavy.
Most of Earth's argon was produced by the radioactive decay of potassium-40 in rocks.
Welders shield hot metal with argon, and it fills many incandescent light bulbs.
from: Argon-36 and argon-38 form in massive stars, but nearly all argon on Earth is argon-40.
Argon-40 comes from the slow radioactive decay of potassium-40 in rocks and makes up nearly 1 percent of air.
It is obtained as a byproduct of the fractional distillation of liquid air.
uses: Argon shields molten metal from air in welding, steelmaking and metal refining.
Light bulbs and fluorescent tubes are filled with argon to protect their electrodes and filaments.
Insulated double-glazed windows use argon between the panes to slow heat loss.
Argon provides an inert atmosphere for growing silicon crystals and producing titanium.
Argon-argon dating measures the ages of volcanic rocks and meteorites.

origin: English: pot ash; symbol from Latin: kalium, (alkali).
h: Potassium is so reactive that it bursts into a lilac-colored flame when dropped into water.
f: Humphry Davy isolated it in 1807, the first metal ever isolated by electrolysis.
Its symbol, K, comes from 'kalium', a name rooted in the Arabic word for plant ashes.
A small fraction of natural potassium is radioactive potassium-40, so every human body is slightly radioactive.
Bananas are famous for it, but potatoes, beans and leafy greens are rich sources too.
from: Potassium forms in massive stars during oxygen burning and is released in supernovae.
It is common in feldspars and micas, while soluble salts such as sylvite are mined as potash.
Canada is the leading potash producer, followed by Russia and Belarus.
Humphry Davy first isolated it in 1807 by electrolysis; today the metal is made by reducing potassium chloride with sodium.
uses: Most potash goes into fertilizer, since potassium is a major plant nutrient.
Potassium hydroxide makes soft soaps and is the electrolyte in alkaline batteries.
Potassium nitrate is an oxidizer in gunpowder, fireworks and some food curing.
Potassium chloride serves as a salt substitute and a medical supplement.
Potassium carbonate is used to make specialty glass, such as for older TV screens and lab glassware.

origin: Latin: calx, calcis (lime).
h: Calcium is the most abundant metal in the human body, mostly stored in bones and teeth.
f: Limestone, marble and chalk are all calcium carbonate, much of it from the shells of ancient sea creatures.
Calcium ions trigger muscle contraction, including every beat of your heart.
Pure calcium is a soft, silvery metal that reacts steadily with water, releasing hydrogen.
Cement and concrete depend on lime, made by heating limestone in kilns.
from: Calcium forms in massive stars during oxygen and silicon burning, and some calcium-40 comes from decay of potassium-40.
It is the fifth most abundant element in the crust, found in limestone, chalk, marble, gypsum and fluorite.
Limestone is quarried worldwide and heated to make lime, calcium oxide.
The metal is produced by reducing lime with aluminum in a vacuum or by electrolysis of calcium chloride.
uses: Limestone is the main raw material for cement and is crushed for construction aggregate.
Lime removes impurities in steelmaking and neutralizes acidic soils and water.
Gypsum, calcium sulfate, makes plaster and drywall.
Calcium carbonate fills paper, plastics and paint and is sold as an antacid and dietary supplement.
Calcium metal deoxidizes steel and helps reduce other metals such as uranium.

origin: Latin: Scandia, Scandinavia.
h: Mendeleev predicted scandium in 1871 as 'eka-boron', and when it was found in 1879, it closely matched his forecast.
f: Lars Fredrik Nilson discovered it in Sweden and named it after Scandinavia.
A dash of scandium makes aluminum alloys stronger, used in some bicycle frames and baseball bats.
It is widespread in Earth's crust but rarely concentrated, which makes it costly to produce.
Scandium iodide is added to some metal-halide lamps to make light resembling sunlight.
from: Scandium is made in supernovae but only in small amounts, so it is relatively scarce in the cosmos.
It is widely scattered in Earth's crust and seldom concentrated, with thortveitite one of few scandium-rich minerals.
Most scandium is recovered as a byproduct from residues of rare earth, uranium, titanium and nickel processing.
Mendeleev predicted it as eka-boron, and Lars Fredrik Nilson discovered it in 1879.
uses: Small additions of scandium refine the grain of aluminum alloys for aerospace parts and sports gear such as bike frames.
Scandium-stabilized zirconia is the electrolyte in some solid oxide fuel cells.
Scandium iodide in metal halide lamps gives a light close to sunlight for stadiums and film sets.

origin: Greek: titanos (Titans).
h: Titanium is as strong as many steels but around 45 percent lighter, making it prized for aircraft and spacecraft.
f: The body tolerates titanium well, so it is used for hip replacements and dental implants.
Titanium dioxide is the brilliant white pigment in paints, paper, toothpaste and sunscreen.
Klaproth named it after the Titans of Greek mythology in 1795.
It is common in Earth's crust, but extracting the pure metal is difficult and expensive.
from: Titanium is made in supernovae, and radioactive titanium-44 glowing in remnants such as Cassiopeia A traces its creation.
It is the ninth most abundant element in the crust, occurring in ilmenite and rutile, often in beach sands.
China, Mozambique, South Africa and Australia are large producers of titanium minerals.
The Kroll process turns ore into titanium tetrachloride and reduces it with magnesium to porous titanium sponge.
uses: Most titanium ore becomes titanium dioxide, the bright white pigment in paint, paper, plastics and sunscreen.
Strong, light titanium alloys are used in jet engines and airframes.
Its corrosion resistance and compatibility with bone suit hip, knee and dental implants.
Desalination plants, chemical equipment and ship parts use titanium to resist seawater.
Watches, eyeglass frames and bicycles use titanium for its lightness.

origin: From Scandinavian goddess, Vanadis.
h: Vanadium is named after Vanadís, a Norse goddess of beauty, because its compounds come in so many vivid colors.
f: A little vanadium makes steel tough and shock-resistant, ideal for tools and springs.
Henry Ford used vanadium steel in the Model T for its strength and lightness.
Vanadium flow batteries store energy in tanks of liquid, useful for backing up power grids.
Some sea squirts concentrate vanadium in their blood cells to remarkable levels.
from: Vanadium forms in supernova explosions, both of collapsing massive stars and of exploding white dwarfs.
It occurs in titanium-rich magnetite ores, in minerals such as vanadinite and carnotite, and in crude oil.
China, Russia and South Africa produce most vanadium, largely from slag left after smelting titanomagnetite ore.
It is recovered as vanadium pentoxide, then reduced to make ferrovanadium for steelmakers.
uses: Most vanadium strengthens steel for rebar, tools, pipelines and axles.
Titanium alloy with aluminum and vanadium is a standard material for aircraft and medical implants.
Vanadium redox flow batteries store energy for electric grids.
Vanadium pentoxide catalyzes the production of sulfuric acid.

origin: Greek: chrôma (color).
h: Chromium gives rubies their red and emeralds their green; the color depends on the crystal surrounding it.
f: Stainless steel stays shiny because its chromium forms an invisible, self-repairing oxide layer.
Chrome plating gives a mirror-bright, hard-wearing finish to car trim and taps.
Its name comes from the Greek 'chroma', meaning color, after its colorful compounds.
Hexavalent chromium compounds are toxic and cause cancer, while trivalent chromium is far less harmful.
from: Chromium comes from supernovae of both massive stars and white dwarfs, forged in the intense heat of the explosion.
Its only commercial ore is chromite, an iron-chromium oxide.
South Africa mines the most chromite, followed by Kazakhstan, Turkey and India.
Chromite is smelted with carbon to make ferrochromium, while pure chromium comes from aluminothermic reduction or electrolysis.
uses: Most chromium goes into stainless steel, where it forms a thin, self-healing oxide film that blocks rust.
Chrome plating gives faucets, car trim and tools a hard, shiny finish.
Chromium compounds tan most of the world's leather.
Chromium pigments such as chrome green and chrome yellow color paints and ceramics.
Chromite bricks line high-temperature furnaces.

origin: Latin: magnes (magnet); Italian: manganese.
h: Most mined manganese, around 90 percent, goes into making iron and steel, where it adds strength and toughness.
f: Vast fields of manganese-rich nodules lie scattered across the deep ocean floor.
Plants use a manganese cluster to split water during photosynthesis, releasing the oxygen we breathe.
Potassium permanganate forms deep purple solutions used as a disinfectant and oxidizer.
Prehistoric artists used manganese oxides as black pigment in cave paintings.
from: Manganese forms in supernovae, with a large share from thermonuclear explosions of white dwarfs.
Its main ores are pyrolusite and other manganese oxides, and nodules on the deep sea floor also hold large amounts.
South Africa, Gabon and Australia are leading producers.
Ore is smelted with carbon to make ferromanganese and silicomanganese, while pure manganese is made by electrolysis.
uses: About 90 percent of manganese is used in steelmaking to remove sulfur and oxygen and add strength.
Manganese dioxide is the cathode material in alkaline and zinc-carbon batteries.
Some lithium-ion battery cathodes contain manganese.
Aluminum beverage cans contain manganese for strength and corrosion resistance.
Manganese is an essential trace nutrient added to animal feed and fertilizers.

origin: Anglo-Saxon: iron; symbol from Latin: ferrum (iron).
h: Iron is the most abundant element in Earth as a whole by mass, mostly concentrated in the planet's core.
f: Iron in hemoglobin carries oxygen around your body and helps give blood its red color.
Steel, iron alloyed with a little carbon, is the most widely used metal in the world.
Fusion in massive stars stops at iron, because fusing it further consumes energy rather than releasing it.
Its symbol, Fe, comes from the Latin 'ferrum'.
from: Iron is built in massive stars by silicon burning, largely as nickel-56 that decays to iron-56 after a supernova.
Exploding white dwarfs, called type Ia supernovae, produce much of the galaxy's iron.
Iron dominates Earth's core and is the fourth most abundant crustal element, mined mainly as hematite and magnetite.
Australia and Brazil lead iron ore mining, and blast furnaces reduce the ore with coke to make iron.
uses: Steel, iron alloyed with a little carbon, is the most used metal, forming buildings, bridges, cars, ships and machinery.
Cast iron is used for engine blocks, pipes and cookware.
Silicon steel cores in transformers and motors channel magnetic fields efficiently.
Iron oxides are pigments in paints, bricks, concrete and cosmetics.
Iron supplements treat anemia, since hemoglobin needs iron to carry oxygen in blood.

origin: German: kobold (goblin).
h: Cobalt is named after kobolds, mischievous goblins that German miners blamed for troublesome ores that gave off poisonous fumes.
f: Cobalt compounds have colored glass and ceramics a deep 'cobalt blue' for thousands of years.
Vitamin B12 is built around a single cobalt atom.
Cobalt goes into many lithium-ion battery cathodes and heat-resistant superalloys for jet engines.
Radioactive cobalt-60 is used to sterilize medical equipment and to treat cancer.
from: Stable cobalt-59 is forged in supernovae, while radioactive cobalt-56 powers their fading glow for months.
It usually occurs with copper and nickel ores rather than in its own deposits.
The Democratic Republic of the Congo produces most mined cobalt, largely as a byproduct of copper mining.
Cobalt is recovered by leaching and refining, and China does most of the world's refining.
uses: Lithium-ion battery cathodes are now the largest use of cobalt.
Cobalt superalloys withstand heat in jet engine and gas turbine parts.
Cobalt binds tungsten carbide grains in hard cutting tools.
Cobalt blue pigments have colored glass and ceramics for centuries.
Cobalt-60 gamma rays sterilize medical equipment and treat cancer.

origin: German: kupfernickel (false copper).
h: Nickel's name comes from 'Kupfernickel', or 'Old Nick's copper', an ore that German miners thought was bewitched copper.
f: Most nickel goes into stainless steel, where it adds toughness and corrosion resistance.
Iron meteorites are mostly iron–nickel alloy, and Earth's core is thought to be similar.
Like iron and cobalt, nickel is strongly magnetic at room temperature.
The US 'nickel' coin is actually 75 percent copper and only 25 percent nickel.
from: Nickel is forged alongside iron in supernovae, and iron meteorites contain it in large amounts.
Much of Earth's nickel is in the core, but crustal deposits occur as sulfides such as pentlandite and as laterites.
Indonesia is now by far the leading producer, followed by the Philippines and Russia.
It is refined by smelting and electrolysis, or by the Mond process using nickel carbonyl gas.
uses: About two thirds of nickel goes into stainless steel.
Nickel-rich cathodes boost the energy density of electric vehicle batteries.
Nickel superalloys survive extreme heat in jet engine turbines.
Nickel plating protects metal parts, and nickel alloys appear in many coins.
Nickel-metal hydride batteries power many hybrid cars.

origin: Symbol from Latin: cuprum (island of Cyprus famed for its copper mines).
h: Copper was one of the first metals humans used, worked into ornaments and tools more than 9,000 years ago.
f: It conducts electricity better than any metal except silver, so it wires our homes and devices.
The Statue of Liberty is green because its copper skin has weathered to form a patina.
Mixing copper with tin made bronze, which gave the Bronze Age its name.
Octopuses and many mollusks have blue blood, colored by copper-containing hemocyanin.
from: Copper forms partly in supernovae and partly by slow neutron capture in massive stars.
Its main ores are sulfides such as chalcopyrite and chalcocite, and native copper also occurs.
Chile is the largest producer, with Peru, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and China also major sources.
Ores are smelted and refined by electrolysis, or leached and recovered by electrowinning.
uses: Electrical wiring and power cables are the largest use, thanks to copper's high conductivity.
Electric motors, transformers and generators rely on copper windings.
Copper pipes carry water, and copper tubing moves refrigerant in air conditioners.
Brass and bronze alloys make valves, fittings, musical instruments and statues.
Historical: copper was the first metal people widely shaped into tools and ornaments, many thousands of years ago.

origin: German: zink (German for tin).
h: Zinc coatings protect steel from rust by corroding first, sacrificing themselves to save the iron beneath.
f: Brass, used in musical instruments and fittings, is an alloy of copper and zinc.
Hundreds of enzymes in your body need zinc, and it supports immune function.
US pennies made since 1982 are about 97.5 percent zinc, with a thin copper plating.
Zinc oxide is a common mineral sunscreen and a soothing ingredient in diaper creams.
from: Zinc forms in massive stars through the slow neutron-capture process and in supernovae.
Its main ore is sphalerite, a zinc sulfide often found with lead.
China is the largest producer, followed by Peru and Australia.
Concentrates are roasted and leached, then zinc is recovered by electrolysis.
uses: Galvanizing coats steel with zinc to prevent rust and is the largest use.
Zinc alloys are die-cast into hardware, and brass is copper alloyed with zinc.
Zinc oxide is used in rubber manufacturing, sunscreen and skin ointments.
Zinc is the anode in alkaline and zinc-air batteries.
Zinc is an essential nutrient included in supplements and fertilizers.

origin: Latin: Gallia (France).
h: Gallium melts at about 30 °C, so a solid piece will melt in the warmth of your hand.
f: Mendeleev predicted it as 'eka-aluminum'; Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran discovered it in 1875.
Gallium nitride and gallium arsenide are semiconductors in LEDs, lasers and fast electronics.
Once molten, it stays liquid until about 2,400 °C, an enormous liquid range.
Liquid gallium seeps into aluminum, making it brittle enough to crumble.
from: Gallium comes from neutron capture on iron-group nuclei, both in massive stars and in supernovae.
It has no ores of its own and occurs at trace levels in bauxite and zinc ores.
Most gallium is recovered as a byproduct of alumina refining, and China produces the great majority.
Mendeleev predicted it as eka-aluminum before Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran discovered it in 1875.
uses: Gallium nitride makes blue and white LEDs, laser diodes and compact fast chargers.
Gallium arsenide chips handle radio signals in phones and radar and make efficient solar cells for satellites.
Galinstan, an alloy of gallium, indium and tin, replaces mercury in some thermometers.
Gallium-67 and gallium-68 are used in nuclear medicine imaging.

origin: Latin: Germania (Germany).
h: The first transistor, built at Bell Labs in 1947, was made of germanium, before silicon took over electronics.
f: Mendeleev predicted it as 'eka-silicon'; Clemens Winkler found it in 1886 and named it after Germany.
Germanium is transparent to infrared light, so it makes lenses for thermal-imaging cameras.
It is used in fiber-optic cables and in high-efficiency solar cells for satellites.
Most germanium is recovered as a by-product of zinc ore processing and from coal ash.
from: Germanium builds up as massive stars slowly capture neutrons on iron seed nuclei, with supernovae adding more.
It is scattered through zinc ores and some coal deposits rather than forming ores of its own.
It is recovered from zinc refining residues and coal fly ash, and China is the leading producer.
Mendeleev predicted it as eka-silicon, and Clemens Winkler isolated it in 1886.
uses: Germanium dioxide raises the refractive index of the light-carrying core of optical fibers.
Germanium lenses and windows transmit infrared light in thermal imaging cameras.
Multijunction solar cells on satellites are built on germanium wafers.
Germanium detectors measure gamma-ray energies with high precision.
Historical: the first transistor, built at Bell Labs in 1947, used germanium.

origin: Greek: arsenikon; Latin: arsenicum, (both names for yellow pigment).
h: Arsenic was so popular with poisoners that it earned the grim nickname 'inheritance powder'.
f: The Marsh test, devised in 1836, gave forensic scientists a reliable way to detect arsenic.
Salvarsan, an arsenic compound introduced in 1910 to treat syphilis, was one of the first modern drugs.
Bright green arsenic pigments colored 19th-century wallpapers, paints and even clothing.
Groundwater naturally contaminated with arsenic affects millions of people, notably in Bangladesh.
from: Arsenic, which has a single stable isotope, is built by neutron capture in stars and stellar explosions.
It occurs in minerals such as arsenopyrite, realgar and orpiment, often alongside copper, gold and lead ores.
It is recovered as arsenic trioxide from smelter dust, and China is a leading producer.
Natural arsenic contaminates groundwater in some regions, notably Bangladesh and parts of India.
uses: Gallium arsenide semiconductors are used in microwave electronics, LEDs and solar cells.
Small amounts of arsenic harden lead alloys in batteries and ammunition.
Arsenic trioxide is an approved drug for acute promyelocytic leukemia.
Historical: arsenic compounds were widely used as pesticides, wood preservatives and a notorious poison.
Historical: Scheele's green and Paris green, arsenic pigments, colored wallpaper and paint in the 1800s.

origin: Greek: selênê (moon).
h: Selenium conducts electricity better in light than in darkness, a discovery that led to early light meters and photocopiers.
f: Jöns Jacob Berzelius discovered it in 1817 and named it after Selene, the Greek moon goddess.
Your body needs a trace of selenium, but only a little more becomes toxic.
Brazil nuts are among the richest food sources of selenium.
It is added to glass to cancel greenish tints or to color it red.
from: Selenium is built by neutron capture, mostly in massive stars and their explosions.
It occurs mostly in copper sulfide ores, where it substitutes for sulfur.
It is recovered from the anode slimes left after electrolytic refining of copper.
Jöns Jacob Berzelius discovered it in 1817 and named it after the Moon.
uses: Selenium removes the green tint from glass, and larger amounts give glass a red color.
Selenium dioxide improves the electrolytic production of manganese metal.
Selenium is an essential trace nutrient added to animal feed and dietary supplements.
Selenium sulfide is an active ingredient in anti-dandruff shampoos.
Historical: selenium-coated drums were the light-sensitive heart of early photocopiers and laser printers.

origin: Greek: brômos (stench).
h: Bromine is one of only two elements that are liquid at room temperature; the other is mercury.
f: It is a dark red-brown liquid with choking fumes; its name comes from the Greek for 'stench'.
Most bromine is extracted from salty brines and seawater, including the Dead Sea.
Tyrian purple, the ancient dye of royalty, is a bromine compound made by sea snails.
Bromine compounds have been widely used as flame retardants in plastics and textiles.
from: Bromine, unlike the lighter halogens, comes mainly from neutron capture in stars and stellar explosions.
It occurs as bromide salts in seawater and is especially concentrated in the Dead Sea and some underground brines.
The United States, Israel, Jordan and China are leading producers.
Chlorine oxidizes the bromide in brine to bromine, which is stripped out with air or steam.
uses: Brominated flame retardants reduce the fire risk of plastics in electronics, furniture and insulation.
Dense calcium and zinc bromide brines are used as fluids in oil and gas wells.
Bromine compounds disinfect hot tubs and treat industrial cooling water.
Silver bromide is the light-sensitive compound in most photographic film.
Historical: ethylene dibromide was added to leaded gasoline to clear lead deposits from engines.

who: Sir William Ramsay, M. W. Travers
origin: Greek: kryptos (hidden).
h: From 1960 to 1983, the meter was officially defined by the orange-red light given off by krypton-86 atoms.
f: Ramsay and Travers discovered it in 1898; its name comes from the Greek 'kryptos', meaning hidden.
It makes up only about one part per million of Earth's air.
It is used in some flash lamps and as insulating gas between panes of energy-efficient windows.
Despite being a noble gas, it can form a compound with fluorine, krypton difluoride.
from: Krypton is made by slow neutron capture in giant stars and by supernovae.
It is a trace gas in the atmosphere, at about one part per million.
It is extracted as a byproduct of liquid air distillation.
Some radioactive krypton-85 in air comes from reprocessing of nuclear fuel.
uses: Krypton fills high-performance insulated windows and some light bulbs.
Krypton fluoride excimer lasers are used in chipmaking and laser fusion research.
Krypton is a cheaper propellant than xenon for some satellite ion thrusters.
Historical: from 1960 to 1983 the meter was defined by a wavelength of light from krypton-86.

origin: Latin: rubidus (deep red); the color its salts impart to flames.
h: Rubidium atoms tick inside compact atomic clocks used in GPS satellites and telecommunications networks.
f: Bunsen and Kirchhoff discovered it in 1861 by spotting deep red lines in a mineral's spectrum.
Its name comes from the Latin 'rubidus', meaning deep red.
It melts at about 39 °C and catches fire spontaneously in air.
In 1995, rubidium atoms were used to create the first Bose–Einstein condensate, a strange new state of matter.
from: Rubidium is made by both slow and rapid neutron capture, and part of it is radioactive rubidium-87.
It has no ores of its own and occurs in lepidolite and pollucite, alongside lithium and cesium.
It is recovered in small quantities as a byproduct of lithium and cesium processing.
Robert Bunsen and Gustav Kirchhoff discovered it in 1861 from its deep red spectral lines.
uses: Rubidium atomic clocks keep precise time in cell towers, networks and GPS satellites.
Laser-cooled rubidium atoms formed the first Bose-Einstein condensate in 1995.
Rubidium-strontium dating measures the ages of very old rocks and meteorites.
Rubidium-82 is used in PET scans of blood flow in the heart.

origin: From the Scottish town, Strontian.
h: Strontium salts give fireworks and emergency flares their brilliant crimson red color.
f: It is named after Strontian, a Scottish village where its mineral was first found.
The body treats strontium much like calcium, taking it up into bones.
Radioactive strontium-90 from nuclear fallout is a health hazard because it lodges in bone.
Strontium isotopes in ancient teeth help archaeologists trace where people grew up.
from: Strontium is made mostly by slow neutron capture in giant stars.
Astronomers reported strontium in the debris of a neutron star merger observed in 2017.
Its main ores are celestine, strontium sulfate, and strontianite, strontium carbonate.
It is named after Strontian, the Scottish village where its mineral was first found.
uses: Strontium salts give fireworks and road flares a bright red color.
Strontium ferrite forms permanent magnets in small motors and loudspeakers.
Strontium aluminate makes long-lasting glow-in-the-dark paints and signs.
Strontium-89 relieves pain from cancer that has spread to bone.
Historical: strontium in color TV glass blocked X-rays from cathode ray tubes.

origin: From the Swedish village, Ytterby, where one of its minerals was first found.
h: Yttrium is one of four elements named after Ytterby, a single small mining village in Sweden.
f: Johan Gadolin identified its oxide in 1794 from a black mineral found near Ytterby.
Yttrium-based phosphors produced the red glow in old color-television picture tubes.
Yttrium barium copper oxide was the first superconductor to work above liquid nitrogen's boiling point.
Lasers built from yttrium aluminum garnet crystals, known as YAG lasers, are used in surgery and industry.
from: Yttrium belongs to the first abundance peak of slow neutron capture, building up in aging giant stars.
It occurs with rare earths in xenotime, monazite and ion-adsorption clays.
China dominates production, especially from ion-adsorption clays in the south.
It is named after Ytterby, a Swedish village whose quarry gave names to four elements.
uses: Yttria-stabilized zirconia is used in thermal barrier coatings, dental crowns and oxygen sensors.
Yttrium aluminum garnet crystals host neodymium in widely used industrial and medical lasers.
Yttrium compounds in phosphors turn blue LED light into white light.
Yttrium barium copper oxide was the first superconductor to work above the boiling point of liquid nitrogen.
Yttrium-90 beads deliver radiation therapy to liver tumors.

origin: From the mineral, zircon.
h: Zirconium barely absorbs neutrons, so it sheathes the uranium fuel inside most nuclear reactors.
f: Zircon grains about 4.4 billion years old from Western Australia are among the oldest known Earth minerals.
Cubic zirconia, a sparkling diamond imitation, is made from zirconium dioxide.
It resists corrosion extremely well, even in many strong acids and alkalis.
Its name comes from zircon, a gemstone known since ancient times.
from: Zirconium is made mainly by slow neutron capture, and giant stars rich in zirconium oxide show the process at work.
Its main mineral is zircon, found in heavy mineral beach sands; Australia and South Africa lead production.
Zircon grains from Western Australia over 4 billion years old are the oldest known pieces of Earth.
The metal is made by the Kroll process, and hafnium must be removed for nuclear uses.
uses: Zircon makes ceramic tiles and sinks opaque white and lines foundry molds.
Zircaloy tubes clad nuclear fuel because zirconium barely absorbs neutrons.
Cubic zirconia is a diamond-like gemstone, and zirconia makes tough ceramic knives and dental crowns.
Zirconium resists corrosion in chemical plant equipment.

origin: From Niobe; daughter of the mythical Greek king Tantalus.
h: Niobium–titanium wire forms the superconducting magnets in most MRI scanners and in the Large Hadron Collider.
f: It is named after Niobe, daughter of Tantalus, because it is so chemically similar to tantalum.
Small amounts of niobium strengthen the steel used in pipelines, cars and bridges.
Brazil produces the great majority of the world's niobium.
Charles Hatchett discovered it in 1801 and called it columbium, a name used in America for decades.
from: Niobium comes mainly from slow neutron capture, partly through the decay of radioactive zirconium-93.
Its main ore is pyrochlore, often found in carbonatite rocks.
Brazil produces about 90 percent of the world's niobium, with Canada a distant second.
Pyrochlore concentrate is reduced with aluminum to make ferroniobium for steelmakers.
uses: Tiny additions of niobium strengthen steel for pipelines, car bodies and bridges.
Niobium-titanium wire forms the superconducting magnets in MRI scanners and particle accelerators.
Niobium alloys are used in jet engine parts and rocket nozzles.
Pure niobium makes superconducting radio-frequency cavities that accelerate particle beams.

origin: Greek: molybdos (lead).
h: Molybdenum melts at about 2,620 °C, and adding it to steel helps the steel stay strong when red-hot.
f: Its name comes from the Greek for lead, because its ore was long confused with lead ore and graphite.
Nitrogen-fixing bacteria rely on a molybdenum-containing enzyme to turn air into usable nitrogen.
Molybdenum disulfide is a slippery solid lubricant, much like graphite.
Scheele identified it in 1778, and Peter Jacob Hjelm isolated the metal in 1781.
from: Molybdenum comes from slow and rapid neutron capture, plus an unusually large share of proton-rich isotopes of debated origin.
Its chief ore is molybdenite, molybdenum disulfide, often found in porphyry copper deposits.
China is the leading producer, followed by Peru, Chile and the United States.
Molybdenite is roasted to molybdenum trioxide, which is reduced to ferromolybdenum or pure metal.
uses: Most molybdenum alloys steel, improving strength, heat resistance and corrosion resistance.
Molybdenum catalysts remove sulfur from petroleum products.
Molybdenum disulfide is a slippery solid lubricant for engines and machinery.
Molybdenum-99 decays into technetium-99m, the workhorse isotope of medical imaging.
It is an essential trace element for enzymes, including those that let bacteria fix nitrogen.

origin: Greek: technêtos (artificial).
h: Technetium was the first element made artificially, and its name comes from the Greek word for 'artificial'.
f: Carlo Perrier and Emilio Segrè found it in 1937 in molybdenum bombarded in a cyclotron.
It has no stable isotopes, so any technetium present when Earth formed has long since decayed.
Technetium-99m is the workhorse of medical imaging, used in tens of millions of scans every year.
Its detection in some red giant stars proved that stars forge heavy elements.
from: Every technetium isotope is radioactive, so any present when Earth formed has long since decayed.
Its spectral lines in some red giant stars showed in 1952 that stars make heavy elements.
Tiny traces form on Earth from spontaneous fission of uranium.
Carlo Perrier and Emilio Segrè identified it in 1937 in cyclotron-bombarded molybdenum; it now comes from reactors.
uses: Technetium-99m is the most widely used medical radioisotope, used in tens of millions of scans each year.
Chemists attach it to many carrier molecules to image bones, heart, thyroid, kidneys and lungs.
Research: long-lived technetium-99 from spent fuel is studied because it moves easily through groundwater.

origin: Latin: Ruthenia (Russia).
h: Ruthenium was the last platinum-group metal to be discovered, and it is named after Ruthenia, a Latin name for Russia.
f: Karl Ernst Claus isolated it in 1844 at Kazan University from platinum ore residues.
It is used in hard-wearing electrical contacts and in thin layers inside computer hard drives.
Ruthenium-based Grubbs catalysts were part of the work honored by the 2005 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
It is one of the rarest metals in Earth's crust.
from: Ruthenium is made mostly by the rapid neutron-capture process in neutron star mergers and supernovae.
It occurs with other platinum group metals, mainly in South Africa's Bushveld Complex and Russian nickel ores.
It is separated as a byproduct of platinum and nickel refining.
Karl Ernst Claus isolated it in 1844 and named it after Ruthenia, a Latin name for Russia.
uses: Ruthenium is used in chip resistors, electrical contacts and thin layers in hard disk drives.
Ruthenium-coated titanium anodes produce chlorine in chlor-alkali plants.
Ruthenium catalysts are used in ammonia synthesis and fine chemical production.
Small additions harden platinum and palladium jewelry alloys.

origin: Greek: rhodon (rose). Its salts give a rosy solution.
h: Rhodium is one of the rarest and most expensive precious metals, vital to catalytic converters that clean car exhaust.
f: Its name comes from the Greek 'rhodon', meaning rose, after the color of its salts.
William Hyde Wollaston discovered it in 1803 while purifying platinum.
A thin rhodium plating gives white gold and silver jewelry a bright, tarnish-resistant shine.
Most rhodium comes from South Africa, as a by-product of platinum mining.
from: Rhodium's single stable isotope, rhodium-103, is made mostly by rapid neutron capture.
It is one of the rarest stable elements in Earth's crust, found with platinum and nickel ores.
South Africa supplies most of the world's rhodium as a byproduct of platinum mining.
William Hyde Wollaston discovered it in 1803 and named it for the rose color of its salts.
uses: Catalytic converters use rhodium to break down nitrogen oxides in car exhaust; this is its largest use.
Rhodium catalysts help make chemicals such as acetic acid and the aldehydes used in plastics.
Rhodium plating gives white gold jewelry a bright, durable finish.
Platinum-rhodium alloys make thermocouples and the bushings used to spin glass fiber.

origin: Named after the asteroid, Pallas, discovered in 1803.
h: Palladium can soak up around 900 times its own volume of hydrogen gas, like a metal sponge.
f: Wollaston discovered it in 1803 and named it after the asteroid Pallas, found the year before.
Most palladium goes into catalytic converters, turning toxic exhaust gases into less harmful ones.
Palladium catalysts help chemists join carbon atoms, work honored by the 2010 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
It is also used in electronics, dentistry and white gold jewelry.
from: Palladium is made by slow and rapid neutron capture, and meteorites record its extinct radioactive isotope palladium-107.
It occurs with platinum and nickel ores; Russia and South Africa are the leading producers.
It is refined as a byproduct of nickel mining at Norilsk and platinum mining in the Bushveld Complex.
Wollaston discovered it in 1802 and named it after the newly found asteroid Pallas.
uses: Catalytic converters in gasoline cars use most of the world's palladium.
Multilayer ceramic capacitors and connectors in electronics use palladium.
Dental alloys and white gold jewelry contain palladium.
Palladium-catalyzed coupling reactions, honored by the 2010 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, help make many drugs.
Palladium absorbs large amounts of hydrogen and is used to purify it.

origin: Anglo-Saxon: siolful, (silver); symbol from Latin: argentium.
h: Silver is the best electrical conductor of all the elements and reflects more visible light than any other metal.
f: Light-sensitive silver halide crystals made film photography possible.
Silver ions kill many bacteria, so silver is used in some wound dressings.
Its symbol, Ag, comes from the Latin 'argentum', and Argentina is named after the metal.
Silver tarnishes black when it reacts with traces of sulfur compounds in the air.
from: Silver is produced mostly by rapid neutron capture, though its exact cosmic sources are still debated.
It occurs as native silver and in sulfide minerals, often alongside lead, zinc, copper and gold ores.
Mexico is the largest producer, followed by China and Peru.
Most silver is recovered as a byproduct of mining other metals and refined by electrolysis.
uses: Silver paste forms the electrical contacts on most solar cells, now a leading use.
Electronics use silver in contacts, switches and conductive inks because it conducts best of all metals.
Jewelry, silverware, coins and bullion remain major uses.
Silver compounds kill bacteria and are used in wound dressings and water filters.
Historical: film photography consumed huge amounts of silver before digital cameras took over.

origin: Greek: kadmeia (ancient name for calamine (zinc oxide)).
h: Cadmium yellows and reds are brilliant, long-lasting artists' pigments, popular with painters since the 19th century.
f: Friedrich Stromeyer discovered it in 1817 as an impurity in zinc carbonate.
Rechargeable nickel–cadmium batteries were widely used before lithium-ion batteries took over.
Cadmium is highly toxic; contaminated rice caused Japan's painful 'itai-itai' bone disease.
It absorbs neutrons strongly, so it is used in some nuclear reactor control rods.
from: Cadmium is built largely by slow neutron capture in aging giant stars.
It occurs in small amounts in zinc ores, and greenockite is its only notable mineral.
It is recovered almost entirely as a byproduct of zinc refining.
Friedrich Stromeyer discovered it in 1817 as an impurity in zinc carbonate.
uses: Cadmium telluride thin-film solar panels are made on a large scale.
Nickel-cadmium rechargeable batteries were long its main use but are being phased out.
Cadmium pigments give bright yellows, oranges and reds to artists' paints and plastics.
Cadmium absorbs neutrons and is used in some nuclear reactor control rods.
Cadmium plating protects steel aircraft parts from corrosion.

origin: Latin: indicum (color indigo), the color it shows in a spectroscope.
h: Indium tin oxide is a transparent conductor of electricity, which makes touchscreens and flat-panel displays possible.
f: It was discovered in 1863 and named for the bright indigo line in its spectrum.
Indium is so soft that it can be scratched with a fingernail.
It sticks to glass and makes airtight seals in cryogenic and vacuum equipment.
Most indium is recovered as a by-product of zinc refining.
from: Indium comes from neutron capture in stars, and most natural indium is the extremely slowly decaying indium-115.
It occurs in trace amounts in zinc sulfide ores.
It is recovered as a byproduct of zinc refining, and China is the leading producer, followed by South Korea.
Ferdinand Reich and Theodor Richter discovered it in 1863 from its indigo spectral line.
uses: Indium tin oxide forms the transparent conducting layer in touchscreens and flat-panel displays.
Indium solders and alloys bond at low temperatures and seal cryogenic equipment.
Indium phosphide lasers and detectors carry signals in fiber optic networks.
Copper indium gallium selenide makes thin-film solar cells.

origin: Named after Etruscan god, Tinia; symbol from Latin: stannum (tin).
h: Bending a bar of tin makes an eerie crackling sound, called 'tin cry', as its crystals slip and twin.
f: Combined with copper, tin makes bronze, the alloy that gave the Bronze Age its name.
Below about 13 °C, shiny tin can slowly crumble into gray powder, a change called 'tin pest'.
'Tin cans' are actually steel coated with a thin protective layer of tin.
Its symbol, Sn, comes from the Latin 'stannum'.
from: Tin is built by neutron capture in stars and has ten stable isotopes, more than any other element.
Its main ore is cassiterite, tin oxide, often found in river gravels.
China, Indonesia and Myanmar are leading producers.
Cassiterite is smelted with carbon to make tin metal.
uses: Solder for joining electronic components is the largest use of tin.
Tinplate coats steel food cans to prevent corrosion.
Tin compounds stabilize PVC plastic and act as industrial catalysts.
Molten tin is the bath on which float glass is formed into flat window panes.
Bronze, an alloy of copper and tin, gave its name to the Bronze Age.

origin: Greek: anti and monos (not alone); symbol from mineral stibnite.
h: Antimony sulfide was used as black eye makeup in the ancient world, giving antimony its symbol, Sb, from 'stibium'.
f: Antimony compounds are widely used as flame retardants in plastics, textiles and electronics.
Added to lead, it hardens the alloy for car batteries and, historically, for printing type.
Unusually, antimony expands slightly as it solidifies, which helped type metal cast crisp letters.
It is a brittle, silvery solid with properties partway between a metal and a nonmetal.
from: Antimony comes from a blend of slow neutron capture in giant stars and rapid capture in explosive events.
Its main ore is stibnite, antimony sulfide.
China produces about half of the world's antimony, with Russia and Tajikistan also significant.
Stibnite is roasted to an oxide and reduced with carbon, or melted and reduced with iron.
uses: Antimony trioxide boosts halogenated flame retardants in plastics and textiles.
Antimony hardens lead in car batteries, bullets and cable sheathing.
Antimony compounds catalyze the production of PET plastic for bottles.
Antimony is added to some glass to remove bubbles, including in solar panel cover glass.
Historical: ancient peoples used powdered stibnite as a black eye cosmetic.

origin: Latin: tellus (earth).
h: Absorbing even a tiny amount of tellurium can give a person garlicky 'tellurium breath' that lingers for weeks.
f: Its name comes from 'tellus', the Latin word for Earth.
It is one of the rarest stable elements in Earth's crust.
Cadmium telluride is used to make thin-film solar panels.
Most tellurium is recovered as a by-product of copper refining.
from: Tellurium is made mostly by rapid neutron capture, and astronomers detected it in a neutron star merger in 2023.
It is one of the rarest stable elements in Earth's crust and is sometimes found in gold telluride minerals.
Most tellurium is recovered from anode slimes in copper refining, and China is the leading producer.
uses: Cadmium telluride solar panels are now a leading use.
Bismuth telluride thermoelectric devices turn heat into electricity or cool small devices.
Small tellurium additions make steel and copper easier to machine.
Tellurium compounds have been used in rewritable optical discs and rubber vulcanization.

origin: Greek: iôeides (violet colored).
h: When warmed, iodine's dark crystals give off a striking violet vapor, which inspired its name, from the Greek for violet.
f: Bernard Courtois discovered it in 1811 while extracting chemicals for gunpowder from seaweed ash.
Your thyroid gland needs iodine to make hormones, so many countries add it to table salt.
Iodine solutions are a classic antiseptic for cleaning skin and wounds.
Iodine turns starch a deep blue-black, a classic chemistry test.
from: Iodine is made mainly by rapid neutron capture in neutron star mergers and supernovae.
It is found in seawater, seaweed, underground brines and as iodate in Chile's nitrate deposits.
Chile produces most of the world's iodine, with Japan second from natural gas brines.
Bernard Courtois discovered it in 1811 in seaweed ash.
uses: Iodine-based contrast agents make blood vessels and organs visible in X-ray and CT scans.
Iodized salt prevents iodine deficiency, which can cause goiter and impaired brain development.
Iodine solutions and povidone-iodine disinfect skin and wounds.
Radioactive iodine-131 treats thyroid cancer and an overactive thyroid.
Iodine is used in LCD polarizing films and as an industrial catalyst.

who: Sir William Ramsay, M. W. Travers
origin: Greek: xenos (strange).
h: Xenon was the first noble gas made to form a chemical compound, in 1962, overturning the belief that these gases were inert.
f: It makes up only about 90 parts per billion of Earth's air.
Xenon flash lamps and some car headlights produce intense, bright white light.
Xenon ion engines gently but efficiently pushed spacecraft such as NASA's Dawn probe.
Inhaled xenon works as a general anesthetic.
from: Xenon's nine natural isotopes come from slow and rapid neutron capture, plus rare proton-rich processes.
It is very rare in the atmosphere, less than a tenth of a part per million.
It is extracted from liquid air in large air separation plants.
Some xenon isotopes come from decay of iodine and plutonium, helping date events in the early solar system.
uses: Xenon ion thrusters propel many satellites and deep-space probes.
Xenon arc lamps make bright white light for cinema projectors and some car headlights.
Xenon can act as a general anesthetic with few side effects, though cost limits its use.
Large tanks of liquid xenon serve as dark matter detectors deep underground.

origin: Latin: coesius (sky blue); for the blue lines of its spectrum.
h: The second is officially defined by cesium-133 atoms: exactly 9,192,631,770 cycles of a microwave frequency characteristic of the atom.
f: It melts at about 28 °C, so it can turn liquid on a hot day.
Cesium reacts explosively with cold water, even more violently than potassium.
Bunsen and Kirchhoff discovered it in 1860 from sky-blue lines in mineral water's spectrum.
Radioactive cesium-137 from the Chernobyl and Fukushima accidents remains a long-term contamination concern.
from: Cesium's only stable isotope, cesium-133, is made mostly by rapid neutron capture.
Its main ore is pollucite, mined chiefly at the Tanco mine in Manitoba, Canada, and in Zimbabwe and Australia.
Pollucite is processed into cesium salts, and the metal is made by reducing them.
Bunsen and Kirchhoff discovered it in 1860 in mineral water from its blue spectral lines.
uses: Cesium formate brine is a dense, low-toxicity drilling fluid for high-pressure oil and gas wells.
Cesium atomic clocks define the second as 9,192,631,770 oscillations of cesium-133.
Cesium-137 is used in industrial gauges, well logging and some radiation therapy devices.
Cesium compounds are used in photoelectric cells and specialty glass.

origin: Greek: barys (heavy or dense).
h: Patients drink a barium sulfate 'milkshake' so their digestive tract shows up clearly on X-rays.
f: Barium sulfate is safe because it barely dissolves, but soluble barium compounds are poisonous.
Barium compounds give fireworks their green color.
Its name comes from the Greek 'barys', meaning heavy, after the dense mineral baryte.
Humphry Davy isolated the metal by electrolysis in 1808.
from: Barium is made mostly by slow neutron capture, and so-called barium stars inherited extra barium from giant companions.
Its main mineral is barite, barium sulfate; China and India are leading producers.
Barite is mostly mined and ground for direct use, and other barium compounds are made by reducing it with carbon.
uses: Ground barite weights drilling mud to control pressure in oil and gas wells, its dominant use.
Barium sulfate coats the digestive tract so it shows up in X-ray examinations.
Barium compounds give fireworks a green color.
Barium titanate is the dielectric in many ceramic capacitors.
Barium ferrite makes cheap permanent magnets and has been used in magnetic stripe cards.

origin: Greek: lanthanein (to be hidden).
h: Lanthanum gives its name to the lanthanides, the 15 metals running from lanthanum to lutetium.
f: Its name comes from the Greek for 'to lie hidden', as it hid in cerium minerals.
Lanthanum is a major ingredient in the nickel–metal hydride batteries of many hybrid cars.
Lanthanum oxide makes high-quality camera lenses that bend light strongly.
Despite being called a rare earth, it is more abundant in Earth's crust than lead.
from: Lanthanum builds up mostly through slow neutron capture in aging giant stars.
It is a light rare earth element found in bastnäsite and monazite.
China produces most rare earths, and Bayan Obo in Inner Mongolia is the largest deposit.
Rare earths are separated from each other by many stages of solvent extraction.
uses: Lanthanum catalysts help crack crude oil into gasoline in refineries.
Nickel-metal hydride batteries in hybrid cars use lanthanum-rich alloys.
Lanthanum oxide makes high-refractive-index glass for camera lenses.
Lanthanum carbonate is a drug that controls high phosphate levels in kidney disease.
Lanthanum hexaboride cathodes emit electrons in electron microscopes.

who: W. von Hisinger, J. Berzelius, M. Klaproth
origin: Named after the asteroid, Ceres, discovered two years before the element.
h: Cerium is the most abundant rare earth element, and scraping its iron alloy produces the sparks in lighter flints.
f: It was named after the dwarf planet Ceres, discovered two years earlier in 1801.
Cerium oxide is used to polish glass and lenses to a fine finish.
In catalytic converters, cerium oxide stores and releases oxygen to help burn pollutants.
It is a soft, silvery metal that tarnishes quickly in air.
from: Cerium is made mainly by slow neutron capture, near an abundance peak at the magic neutron number 82.
It is the most abundant rare earth element, about as common in the crust as copper.
It is extracted from bastnäsite and monazite, mostly in China.
Cerium is easily separated from other rare earths because it can be oxidized to the +4 state.
uses: Cerium oxide polishes glass, lenses, mirrors and silicon wafers.
Catalytic converters use cerium oxide to store and release oxygen.
Ferrocerium sparks in lighter flints and camping fire starters.
Cerium oxide decolorizes glass and blocks ultraviolet light.

origin: Greek: prasios and didymos (green twin); from its green salts.
h: Praseodymium means 'green twin': it was split from 'didymium', a substance once thought to be a single element.
f: Carl Auer von Welsbach separated didymium into praseodymium and neodymium in 1885.
It is alloyed with neodymium in powerful permanent magnets.
Praseodymium compounds give glass and ceramics yellow and green tints.
Didymium glass in glassblowers' goggles filters the intense yellow glare from hot glass.
from: Praseodymium's single stable isotope comes from a mix of slow and rapid neutron capture.
It occurs in bastnäsite and monazite with other light rare earths, and China dominates its mining and separation.
Carl Auer von Welsbach split it from neodymium in 1885, from a supposed element called didymium.
uses: Praseodymium is blended with neodymium in strong neodymium-iron-boron magnets.
Praseodymium gives glass and ceramic glazes a yellow color.
Didymium glass in welders' and glassblowers' goggles filters out the bright yellow glare of hot glass.

origin: Greek: neos and didymos (new twin).
h: Neodymium magnets are the strongest widely available permanent magnets, packing a powerful pull into tiny sizes.
f: They are found in headphones, hard drives, electric car motors and wind turbines.
Neodymium-doped crystals make powerful lasers, including those inside common green laser pointers.
Neodymium gives glass a purple tint that shifts shade under different lighting.
Its name means 'new twin', after its separation from didymium in 1885.
from: Neodymium forms by neutron capture in stars, and some neodymium-143 comes from the decay of samarium-147.
It is concentrated in bastnäsite, monazite and ion-adsorption clays.
China mines and refines most neodymium, with the United States, Australia and Myanmar also producing it.
Purified neodymium oxide is reduced to metal by molten salt electrolysis.
uses: Neodymium magnets power electric vehicle motors, wind turbines, hard drives and earbuds.
Neodymium-doped YAG lasers cut metal, treat eyes and remove tattoos.
Neodymium gives glass a violet tint and is used in some lamp bulbs to improve color.

who: J. A. Marinsky, L. E. Glendenin, C. D. Coryell
origin: Named for the Greek god, Prometheus.
h: Promethium has no stable isotopes, making it one of only two elements lighter than lead that are entirely radioactive.
f: It was confirmed in 1945 at Oak Ridge, among the products of uranium fission.
It is named after Prometheus, the Titan who stole fire from the gods.
Only tiny traces occur in nature, formed in uranium ores by spontaneous fission.
Promethium-147 has been used in luminous paints and long-lasting miniature nuclear batteries.
from: Promethium has no stable isotopes, so almost none survives in nature.
Minute traces form in uranium ores through spontaneous fission.
It was identified in 1945 at Oak Ridge among the fission products of a nuclear reactor.
Promethium-147 is obtained from spent nuclear fuel or by irradiating neodymium with neutrons.
uses: Promethium-147 serves as a beta source in industrial thickness gauges and research.
Historical: promethium-based luminous paint replaced radium on some watch dials and switches.
Historical: promethium betavoltaic batteries powered some early pacemakers.

origin: Named after the mineral samarskite.
h: Samarium was the first element named, indirectly, after a person: Russian mining official Vasili Samarsky-Bykhovets.
f: Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran isolated it in 1879 from the mineral samarskite.
Samarium–cobalt magnets keep their strength at high temperatures, useful in aerospace and military equipment.
Radioactive samarium-153 is used to ease pain from cancer that has spread to bone.
It absorbs neutrons well, so it is used in some reactor control rods.
from: Samarium is made mostly by rapid neutron capture, with a smaller share from giant stars.
It is extracted from monazite and bastnäsite, mainly in China.
It is named after the mineral samarskite, which honors a Russian mining official.
Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran discovered it in 1879.
uses: Samarium-cobalt magnets stay strong at high temperatures in aerospace and military motors.
Samarium-153 relieves pain from cancer that has spread to bone.
Samarium iodide is a widely used reducing agent in organic chemistry labs.
The slow decay of samarium-147 to neodymium-143 dates ancient rocks and meteorites.

origin: Named for the continent of Europe.
h: Europium, named after Europe, glows red or blue under ultraviolet light and helps color many screens and lamps.
f: Eugène-Anatole Demarçay isolated it in 1901.
Europium compounds that glow under ultraviolet light help protect euro banknotes against forgery.
It is the most reactive of the rare earth metals, tarnishing rapidly in air.
Europium-based phosphors make fluorescent lamps produce more natural-looking white light.
from: Europium is made almost entirely by rapid neutron capture, so astronomers use it to track that process in old stars.
It occurs in bastnäsite and monazite and is one of the scarcer rare earths.
Unlike most rare earths it readily takes a +2 charge, which makes it easier to separate.
Eugène-Anatole Demarçay isolated it in 1901 and named it after Europe.
uses: Europium phosphors made the red in color TV screens and fluorescent lamps.
Europium fluorescence provides anti-counterfeiting marks on euro banknotes.
Europium-doped strontium aluminate is the active ingredient in many glow-in-the-dark products.
Europium absorbs neutrons and has been used in reactor control rods.

origin: Named after the mineral gadolinite.
h: Gadolinium compounds are injected as MRI contrast agents to make blood vessels and tumors stand out.
f: It is magnetic only below about 20 °C, so a chilly room can switch its magnetism on.
It is named after Finnish chemist Johan Gadolin, a pioneer of rare earth research.
Gadolinium-157 captures neutrons more strongly than any other stable isotope.
Jean Charles Galissard de Marignac first detected it in 1880.
from: Gadolinium comes mainly from rapid neutron capture in events such as neutron star mergers.
It is extracted from monazite, bastnäsite and ion-adsorption clays.
It is named after the mineral gadolinite, which honors Finnish chemist Johan Gadolin.
Jean Charles Galissard de Marignac detected it in 1880.
