uses: Gadolinium contrast agents sharpen MRI scans of blood vessels and tumors.
Gadolinium captures neutrons extremely well, so it is mixed into reactor fuel as a burnable poison.
Gadolinium compounds are used in X-ray imaging screens.
Gadolinium added to the Super-Kamiokande water detector helps it spot neutrinos.

origin: Named after Ytterby, a village in Sweden.
h: Terbium compounds glow bright green under ultraviolet light and supply the green in many fluorescent lamps and screens.
f: It is one of four elements named after the Swedish village of Ytterby.
Carl Gustaf Mosander discovered it in 1843.
Terfenol-D, an alloy of terbium, dysprosium and iron, changes shape strongly in a magnetic field.
That shape-changing alloy is used in sonar devices and precision actuators.
from: Terbium, with just one stable isotope, is made almost entirely by rapid neutron capture.
It is extracted mainly from ion-adsorption clays in southern China and from xenotime.
Carl Gustaf Mosander discovered it in 1843 and named it after Ytterby, Sweden.
uses: Terbium is added to neodymium magnets to keep them strong at high temperatures in electric vehicle motors.
Terbium phosphors produce green light in fluorescent lamps and displays.
Terfenol-D, an alloy of terbium, dysprosium and iron, changes shape in a magnetic field for sonar and actuators.

origin: Greek: dysprositos (hard to get at).
h: Dysprosium's name comes from the Greek for 'hard to get at', after years of difficult separation work.
f: Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran identified it in 1886.
Pure dysprosium metal was not isolated until the 1950s, after ion-exchange separation was developed.
A little dysprosium helps neodymium magnets keep their strength in hot electric-car motors and wind turbines.
It absorbs neutrons readily and has been used in nuclear reactor control rods.
from: Dysprosium is made mainly by rapid neutron capture, with a modest contribution from giant stars.
It is mined mainly from ion-adsorption clays in southern China and Myanmar.
Lecoq de Boisbaudran identified it in 1886, but pure samples were made only in the 1950s.
Its name comes from a Greek word meaning hard to get at.
uses: Dysprosium raises the heat tolerance of neodymium magnets in wind turbines and electric vehicles.
Dysprosium iodide in metal halide lamps gives intense light for film and stage lighting.
Dysprosium oxide absorbs neutrons in some reactor control rods.

origin: From Holmia, the Latinized name for Stockholm, Sweden.
h: Holmium has the highest magnetic moment of any naturally occurring element, so it helps concentrate the fields of the strongest magnets.
f: It is named after Holmia, the Latin name for Stockholm.
It was identified in 1878–79, independently by Swiss chemists and by Swedish chemist Per Teodor Cleve.
Holmium lasers are used in surgery, including breaking up kidney stones.
Holmium oxide solutions have sharp absorption peaks, so they are used to calibrate spectrometers.
from: Holmium-165, its only stable isotope, comes overwhelmingly from rapid neutron capture.
It is extracted in small amounts from monazite, xenotime and ion-adsorption clays.
Per Teodor Cleve isolated its oxide in 1879 and named it after Holmia, the Latin name for Stockholm.
uses: Holmium-doped YAG lasers break up kidney stones and treat enlarged prostates.
Holmium has an exceptionally high magnetic moment and is used in pole pieces that concentrate strong magnetic fields.
Holmium oxide glass and solutions are standards for calibrating spectrophotometers.
Holmium tints cubic zirconia and glass yellow or red.

origin: Named after the Swedish town, Ytterby.
h: Erbium-doped fibers amplify the light signals that carry internet traffic through undersea cables.
f: It is one of four elements named after the Swedish village of Ytterby.
Carl Gustaf Mosander discovered it in 1843.
Erbium gives glass and cubic zirconia a delicate pink color.
Erbium lasers are used in dermatology and dentistry.
from: Erbium is forged mostly by rapid neutron capture in violent events such as neutron star mergers.
Its sources include xenotime and euxenite, and it is separated along with other heavy rare earths.
Carl Gustaf Mosander discovered it in 1843 in ore from Ytterby, Sweden.
uses: Erbium-doped fiber amplifiers boost signals in long-distance optical fiber cables, including undersea links.
Erbium lasers are used in dermatology and dentistry.
Erbium oxide gives glass, glazes and some sunglasses a pink color.

origin: From Thule ancient name of Scandinavia.
h: Thulium is named after Thule, a legendary land in the far north often linked with Scandinavia.
f: Per Teodor Cleve discovered it in 1879.
It is one of the rarest of the rare earth elements.
Irradiated thulium can serve as a compact X-ray source for portable devices.
Thulium-doped lasers are used in surgery.
from: Thulium, made mostly by rapid neutron capture, is one of the least abundant rare earths.
It occurs in monazite, xenotime and ion-adsorption clays, mostly processed in China.
Per Teodor Cleve discovered it in 1879 and named it after Thule, a legendary far-northern land.
uses: Thulium fiber lasers are used in surgery, including treatment of kidney stones and prostate disease.
Thulium-170 made in reactors serves as a portable X-ray source.

origin: Named for the Swedish village of Ytterby.
h: Ytterbium atoms power some of the most precise optical atomic clocks ever built.
f: It is one of four elements named after the Swedish village of Ytterby.
Jean Charles Galissard de Marignac discovered it in 1878.
Ytterbium-doped fiber lasers are used to cut and weld metal.
It is a soft, silvery metal that slowly tarnishes in air.
from: Ytterbium comes from a mix of slow neutron capture in giant stars and rapid capture in explosive events.
It is separated from heavy rare earth concentrates, mainly from Chinese ion-adsorption clays.
Jean Charles Galissard de Marignac discovered it in 1878 and named it after Ytterby.
uses: Ytterbium optical lattice clocks are among the most precise clocks ever built.
Ytterbium-doped fiber lasers cut and weld metal in factories.
Ytterbium ions are used as qubits in some trapped-ion quantum computers.
Ytterbium-169 is a gamma-ray source for portable radiography.

origin: Named for the ancient name of Paris, Lutecia.
h: Lutetium, the last of the lanthanides, was named after Lutetia, the Roman name for Paris.
f: Georges Urbain, Carl Auer von Welsbach and Charles James separated it independently around 1907.
It is the densest and hardest of the lanthanide metals.
Lutetium-177 is used in targeted radiotherapy for certain cancers, including prostate cancer.
The slow decay of lutetium-176 is used to date ancient rocks and meteorites.
from: Lutetium is one of the rarest rare earths, and its isotope lutetium-176 forms only by slow neutron capture.
It is recovered in small amounts from monazite and xenotime ores.
Georges Urbain discovered it in 1907 and named it after Lutetia, the Latin name for Paris.
uses: Lutetium-177 linked to targeting molecules treats advanced prostate cancer and neuroendocrine tumors.
Lutetium-based scintillator crystals detect gamma rays in PET scanners.
Lutetium-hafnium dating measures the ages of rocks and meteorites.

origin: From Hafnia, the Latin name of Copenhagen.
h: Hafnium hid inside zirconium minerals for over a century, because the two elements are almost chemically identical.
f: Dirk Coster and George de Hevesy discovered it in 1923, naming it after Hafnia, Latin for Copenhagen.
Unlike zirconium, hafnium absorbs neutrons strongly, so it is used in reactor control rods.
Hafnium oxide is a key insulating layer inside modern computer chips.
It is a lustrous, silvery metal that resists corrosion well.
from: Hafnium is made largely by slow neutron capture, and extinct hafnium-182 records when Earth's core formed.
It always occurs with zirconium, typically a few percent of the zirconium in zircon.
It is a byproduct of making nuclear-grade zirconium, which must be hafnium-free.
Dirk Coster and George de Hevesy discovered it in 1923 and named it after Hafnia, Latin for Copenhagen.
uses: Hafnium absorbs neutrons and is used in control rods, especially in naval reactors.
Hafnium oxide is the gate insulator in modern transistors.
Small amounts of hafnium strengthen nickel superalloys in jet engines.
Plasma cutting torches use hafnium electrode tips.

origin: From king Tantalus of Greek mythology, father of Niobe.
h: Tantalum capacitors pack a lot of electrical storage into tiny spaces, making them common in phones and laptops.
f: Anders Gustaf Ekeberg discovered it in 1802 and named it after Tantalus of Greek myth.
It is extremely corrosion-resistant and well tolerated by the body, so it is used in implants.
Coltan, a tantalum ore, has been linked to conflict in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
It has one of the highest melting points of any metal, about 3,000 °C.
from: Tantalum is made by neutron capture, and its rare isotope tantalum-180m is a nuclear isomer never seen to decay.
Its main ore is tantalite, part of the mineral series traded as coltan.
The Democratic Republic of the Congo and Rwanda produce much of the world's tantalum, with Brazil also significant.
Ore is dissolved in hydrofluoric acid, purified by solvent extraction, and reduced with sodium.
uses: Tantalum capacitors are small and reliable, used in phones, computers and car electronics.
Tantalum strengthens superalloys for jet engines and gas turbines.
Its corrosion resistance suits chemical equipment and surgical implants.
Thin tantalum layers act as diffusion barriers in computer chips.

who: Fausto and Juan José de Elhuyar
origin: Swedish: tung sten (heavy stone): symbol from its German name wolfram.
h: Tungsten has the highest melting point of any metal, about 3,420 °C, which is why it glowed in old light bulbs.
f: Its symbol, W, comes from 'wolfram', an old name linked to its ore, wolframite.
Tungsten carbide is extremely hard and tips drill bits, saw blades and ballpoint pens.
It is almost exactly as dense as gold, so it has been used to fake gold bars.
The Elhuyar brothers first isolated it in Spain in 1783.
from: Tungsten builds up through both slow and rapid neutron capture, in giant stars and in explosive events.
Its main ores are wolframite and scheelite.
China produces most of the world's tungsten.
Ores are converted to ammonium paratungstate, and the resulting oxide is reduced with hydrogen to metal powder.
uses: Tungsten carbide, nearly as hard as diamond, forms drill bits and cutting tools; this is the largest use.
Tungsten has the highest melting point of any metal, ideal for welding electrodes and furnace parts.
Dense tungsten alloys make radiation shielding, balance weights and armor-piercing projectiles.
Historical: tungsten filaments lit incandescent light bulbs for about a century.

who: Walter Noddack, Ida Tacke, Otto Berg
origin: Latin: Rhenus, the Rhine River.
h: Rhenium, found in 1925, was the last stable element to be discovered.
f: Walter Noddack, Ida Tacke and Otto Berg discovered it and named it after the Rhine River.
Only tungsten among the metals has a higher melting point.
Nickel superalloys containing rhenium are used for jet-engine turbine blades.
It is one of the rarest elements in Earth's crust.
from: Rhenium comes mostly from rapid neutron capture, and its isotope rhenium-187 decays very slowly to osmium-187.
It is among the rarest elements in Earth's crust and is recovered from molybdenite in porphyry copper deposits.
Chile is the leading producer.
Walter Noddack, Ida Tacke and Otto Berg discovered it in 1925, the last stable element to be found.
uses: Rhenium-containing nickel superalloys in jet engine turbine blades are its main use.
Platinum-rhenium catalysts produce high-octane gasoline components.
Tungsten-rhenium alloys are used in thermocouples and X-ray tube targets.
Rhenium-osmium dating measures the ages of ores and meteorites.

origin: Greek: osmê (odor).
h: Osmium is the densest naturally occurring element, about twice as dense as lead.
f: Its name comes from the Greek 'osme', meaning smell, after the pungent odor of its oxide.
Smithson Tennant discovered it in 1803 in residues left after dissolving platinum ore.
Osmium tetroxide is highly toxic but is used to stain samples for electron microscopy.
Hard osmium alloys were once used to tip fountain-pen nibs and phonograph needles.
from: Osmium is made mainly by rapid neutron capture, and some osmium-187 comes from decay of rhenium-187.
It occurs with other platinum group metals in ores and natural alloys such as osmiridium.
It is recovered during platinum and nickel refining.
Smithson Tennant discovered it in 1803; it is the densest naturally occurring element.
uses: Hard osmium alloys tip fountain pen nibs and instrument pivots.
Osmium tetroxide stains fats in tissue for electron microscopy.
Osmium tetroxide is a reagent in organic synthesis, adding two hydroxyl groups across double bonds.
Historical: osmium filaments lit some early electric lamps before tungsten replaced them.

who: S. Tennant, A. F. Fourcroy, L. N. Vauquelin, H. V. Collet-Descotils
origin: Latin: iris (rainbow).
h: A worldwide layer of iridium-rich clay marks the asteroid impact that ended the age of dinosaurs, 66 million years ago.
f: It is the most corrosion-resistant metal known.
Its name comes from Iris, Greek goddess of the rainbow, because its salts are so colorful.
Smithson Tennant discovered it in 1803, alongside osmium.
The old international standard meter and kilogram were made of a platinum–iridium alloy.
from: Iridium is made mainly by rapid neutron capture in neutron star mergers and supernovae.
It is extremely rare in Earth's crust because most of it sank into the core.
A worldwide iridium-rich clay layer marks the asteroid impact that ended the age of dinosaurs 66 million years ago.
It is recovered during platinum group metal refining, largely in South Africa.
uses: Iridium oxide catalyzes oxygen production in PEM electrolyzers that make green hydrogen.
Iridium crucibles grow single crystals for electronics and lasers.
Iridium-tipped spark plugs last longer in car engines.
Iridium-192 is a gamma source for industrial radiography and cancer brachytherapy.
Historical: the international prototype meter and kilogram were made of platinum-iridium alloy.

origin: Spanish: platina (little silver).
h: Spanish colonists in South America called platinum 'platina', little silver, and often saw it as a nuisance in gold mining.
f: Catalytic converters use platinum to turn harmful exhaust gases into less harmful ones.
Cisplatin, a platinum compound, is a widely used chemotherapy drug.
It is very dense and highly resistant to tarnish and corrosion.
Most of the world's platinum is mined in South Africa.
from: Platinum, like gold, comes almost entirely from rapid neutron capture in neutron-rich cosmic explosions.
South Africa's Bushveld Complex supplies most of the world's platinum.
Russia and Zimbabwe are the next largest producers.
Concentrates are smelted and refined chemically, often alongside nickel and copper.
uses: Catalytic converters, especially in diesel vehicles, use the largest share of platinum.
Platinum jewelry is prized for its whiteness and durability.
Platinum catalysts refine oil, make nitric acid and drive fuel cells.
Cisplatin and carboplatin are chemotherapy drugs used against many cancers.
Platinum is used in hard disks, glass fiber production and investment bars.

origin: Anglo-Saxon: geolo (yellow); symbol from Latin: aurum (shining dawn).
h: Gold is so malleable that a single gram can be hammered into a sheet about one square meter in area.
f: Gold barely reacts with anything, which is why ancient gold artifacts still gleam today.
Gold's yellow color is caused by relativistic effects on its fast-moving inner electrons.
Electronics use gold on connectors because it conducts well and does not corrode.
Its symbol, Au, comes from the Latin 'aurum'.
from: Gold is made by rapid neutron capture, and neutron star mergers are thought to be a major source.
It occurs mostly as native metal in quartz veins and river placers, often in particles too small to see.
China, Russia and Australia are the leading producers.
Ore is usually leached with cyanide solution, then gold is recovered and refined.
uses: Jewelry consumes about half of newly supplied gold.
Central banks and investors hold gold as bars and coins.
Gold plating on connectors and fine gold bonding wires keep electronics reliable.
Thin gold films reflect infrared light on astronaut visors and spacecraft.
Gold nanoparticles produce the colored line in many rapid diagnostic tests, including pregnancy tests.

origin: From the Roman god Mercury; symbol from Latin: hydrargyrus (liquid silver).
h: Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature, and it was once called quicksilver.
f: Its symbol, Hg, comes from 'hydrargyrum', meaning 'water-silver'.
In 1911, mercury became the first material in which superconductivity was discovered.
Its main ore, cinnabar, is a bright red mineral once ground into vermilion pigment.
Mercury vapor is toxic, so mercury thermometers have largely been phased out.
from: Mercury is made mostly by slow neutron capture in giant stars, with a share from rapid capture.
Its main ore is cinnabar, mercury sulfide; Almadén in Spain was the largest mine in history.
Cinnabar is roasted in air and the mercury vapor is condensed.
China is the leading producer, and much mercury is also recovered from recycled products.
uses: The largest use today is small-scale gold mining, where mercury binds gold but causes serious pollution.
Mercury vapor in fluorescent lamps emits ultraviolet light that phosphors turn into visible light.
Dental amalgam fillings contain mercury, though their use is declining.
Historical: mercury cells produced chlorine and caustic soda; most have been phased out.
Historical: mercury thermometers and barometers were standard for centuries.

origin: Greek: thallos (green twig), for a bright green line in its spectrum.
h: Thallium was nicknamed 'the poisoner's poison' because its salts are tasteless, odorless and deadly.
f: William Crookes discovered it in 1861 by spotting a bright green line in a spectrum.
Its name comes from the Greek 'thallos', meaning a green shoot or twig.
Thallium-201 has long been used in heart scans to show blood flow to the heart muscle.
Once common in rat poisons and insecticides, it is now banned for those uses in many countries.
from: Thallium is made mostly by slow neutron capture, near the end of the process's path at lead and bismuth.
It occurs in trace amounts in sulfide ores of zinc, lead and copper, and in rare minerals such as lorándite.
It is recovered as a byproduct of roasting zinc and lead sulfide ores.
William Crookes discovered it in 1861 from its bright green spectral line.
uses: Thallium-201 is used in nuclear medicine heart stress tests.
Thallium-doped sodium iodide crystals detect gamma rays.
Thallium compounds are used in some infrared optics and specialty glasses.
Historical: thallium sulfate was a rat poison and insecticide until its toxicity led to bans in many countries.

origin: Anglo-Saxon: lead; symbol from Latin: plumbum.
h: Romans made water pipes from lead, and the word 'plumbing' comes from its Latin name, plumbum, also the source of Pb.
f: Lead is toxic, especially to children's developing brains, so leaded gasoline and lead paint were phased out.
Most lead today goes into lead-acid batteries, such as those in cars.
Its density makes lead an effective shield against X-rays and gamma rays.
Uranium and thorium slowly decay into lead, which lets geologists date ancient rocks.
from: Lead is made by slow neutron capture in giant stars, and it is also the end point of uranium and thorium decay.
Its main ore is galena, lead sulfide, often found with zinc and silver.
China and Australia mine the most lead, but most lead used today comes from recycled batteries.
Galena is roasted and smelted, while old batteries are melted down and refined.
uses: Lead-acid batteries for cars and backup power use most of the world's lead.
Lead shields people from X-rays and gamma rays in hospitals and nuclear facilities.
Lead is used in ammunition, cable sheathing, roofing and weights.
Historical: leaded gasoline and lead paint spread lead widely, harming health before being phased out.
Historical: Romans used lead water pipes, and the word plumbing comes from its Latin name, plumbum.

origin: German: bisemutum, (white mass), Now spelled wismut.
h: Bismuth was found to be radioactive in 2003, but its half-life is over a billion times the age of the universe.
f: Bismuth crystals grow in stepped, staircase shapes, with rainbow colors from a thin oxide film.
Bismuth subsalicylate is the active ingredient in the stomach remedy Pepto-Bismol.
Unusually for a heavy metal, it has low toxicity, so it replaces lead in some solders and fishing weights.
It is strongly diamagnetic, meaning it is gently pushed away by magnets.
from: Bismuth is the heaviest element made by slow neutron capture, and it is also made by rapid neutron capture.
Bismuth-209 is radioactive, but its half-life is more than a billion times the age of the universe.
Its main minerals are bismuthinite and native bismuth.
It is mostly a byproduct of lead, tungsten and copper refining, and China is the leading producer.
uses: Bismuth subsalicylate soothes upset stomachs in common over-the-counter remedies.
Bismuth replaces toxic lead in solders, plumbing brass, shot and fishing weights.
Low-melting bismuth alloys trigger fire sprinklers and safety plugs.
Bismuth oxychloride gives cosmetics a pearly shimmer.

origin: Named for Poland, native country of Marie Curie.
h: Marie and Pierre Curie discovered polonium in 1898 and named it after Marie's homeland, Poland.
f: Polonium-210 is so intensely radioactive that a small sample heats itself to hundreds of degrees Celsius.
Polonium heat sources kept the Soviet Lunokhod rovers warm through freezing lunar nights.
It was used to poison former Russian security officer Alexander Litvinenko in London in 2006.
It occurs in tiny amounts in uranium ores but is mostly made by irradiating bismuth in reactors.
from: Polonium forms in the uranium and thorium decay chains, so traces occur in uranium ores.
Marie and Pierre Curie discovered it in 1898 and named it after Poland, Marie's homeland.
It is made in nuclear reactors by bombarding bismuth-209 with neutrons, yielding polonium-210.
uses: Polonium-210 static eliminators remove dust and static charge in industry.
Historical: polonium-beryllium sources supplied neutrons to trigger early atomic bombs.
Historical: polonium-210 heaters kept Soviet Lunokhod moon rovers warm through lunar nights.

who: D. R. Corson, K. R. MacKenzie, E. Segrè
origin: Greek: astatos (unstable).
h: Astatine is so rare and so radioactive that no one has ever seen a visible sample of it.
f: It was first made in 1940 at Berkeley by bombarding bismuth with alpha particles.
Its name comes from the Greek 'astatos', meaning unstable.
Its longest-lived isotope has a half-life of only about eight hours.
Astatine-211 is being studied for targeted alpha-particle therapy against cancer.
from: Astatine is one of the rarest natural elements, formed briefly in uranium and thorium decay chains.
Less than a gram is estimated to exist in Earth's crust at any moment.
It was first made in 1940 at Berkeley by bombarding bismuth-209 with alpha particles, still the main method.
A visible amount has never been gathered, because its own radioactive heat would vaporize it.
uses: Astatine-211 is being tested in targeted alpha therapy for cancer.
Research only: chemists study its poorly understood chemistry, which mixes halogen and metal behavior.

origin: Variation of the name of another element, radium.
h: Radon, a radioactive gas seeping from rocks and soil, is a leading cause of lung cancer after smoking.
f: It is colorless and odorless, so homes in risk areas are checked with simple detectors.
Radon forms from the decay of radium, which itself comes from uranium in the ground.
Friedrich Ernst Dorn discovered it in 1900 as a gas given off by radium.
It is one of the densest gases known at room temperature.
from: Radon forms continuously from the decay of radium in the uranium and thorium decay chains.
It seeps from soil and rock into basements and mines and is a leading cause of lung cancer after smoking.
Its longest-lived isotope, radon-222, has a half-life of about 3.8 days.
Friedrich Ernst Dorn identified it in 1900 as a gas given off by radium.
uses: Radon serves as a natural tracer for studying groundwater flow and air movement.
Historical: radon sealed in tiny gold seeds was implanted to treat tumors.

origin: Named for France, the nation of its discovery.
h: Francium is so unstable that its longest-lived isotope has a half-life of only about 22 minutes.
f: Marguerite Perey discovered it in 1939 at the Curie Institute and named it after France.
Only fleeting traces exist in nature, constantly forming and decaying in uranium and thorium ores.
Scientists study it by trapping small clouds of francium atoms with lasers.
No weighable amount has ever been made, so its bulk properties are predicted, not measured.
from: Francium forms fleetingly in the decay chain of uranium-235, and its longest-lived isotope lasts only about 22 minutes.
Marguerite Perey discovered it in 1939 at the Curie Institute in Paris.
Researchers make it by bombarding gold with oxygen ions and catch small clouds of atoms in laser traps.
A weighable amount has never been produced.
uses: Research only: laser-trapped francium atoms test atomic theory and the weak nuclear force.

origin: Latin: radius (ray).
h: Radium paint made watch dials glow, but many 'Radium Girls' who applied it later suffered and died from radiation poisoning.
f: Marie and Pierre Curie discovered it in 1898, later extracting it from tons of pitchblende ore.
Radium compounds glow faintly blue in the dark from their own radioactivity.
In the early 1900s, quack products added radium to tonics, cosmetics and other goods.
Radium-223 is now used to treat prostate cancer that has spread to bone.
from: Radium forms in the uranium and thorium decay chains, and radium-226 from uranium-238 is the most common isotope.
Uranium ores hold only about a third of a gram of radium for every metric ton of uranium.
Marie and Pierre Curie discovered it in 1898 in pitchblende, and Marie Curie isolated the metal in 1910.
uses: Radium-223 treats prostate cancer that has spread to bone.
Radium-226 targets are irradiated to produce actinium-225 for cancer therapy.
Historical: radium paint made glowing watch dials, and many dial painters suffered radiation poisoning.
Historical: radium was used in early radiotherapy and sold in dangerous health tonics.

origin: Greek: akis, aktinos (ray).
h: Actinium glows a pale blue in the dark, because its intense radioactivity excites the surrounding air.
f: André-Louis Debierne discovered it in 1899 in residues of pitchblende left after the Curies' work.
Its name comes from the Greek 'aktis', meaning ray or beam.
It gives its name to the actinides, the 15 elements from actinium to lawrencium.
Actinium-225 is being developed for targeted alpha-particle therapy against cancer.
from: Actinium occurs in trace amounts in uranium ores as a decay product of uranium-235.
André-Louis Debierne discovered it in 1899 in residues left after extracting uranium from pitchblende.
Actinium-227 is made by neutron irradiation of radium-226 in reactors.
Actinium-225 is obtained from decaying thorium-229 or made with accelerators.
uses: Actinium-225 is a promising alpha emitter in clinical trials of targeted cancer therapy.
Actinium-beryllium sources have supplied neutrons for well logging and research.

origin: Named for Thor, Norse god of thunder.
h: Thorium is three to four times more abundant in Earth's crust than uranium, and it could one day fuel nuclear reactors.
f: Jöns Jacob Berzelius discovered it in 1829 and named it after Thor, Norse god of thunder.
Thorium-232 has a half-life of about 14 billion years, roughly the age of the universe.
Thorium oxide once made gas lantern mantles glow a brilliant white.
Heat from decaying thorium and uranium helps keep Earth's interior hot.
from: Thorium is made by rapid neutron capture, and its 14-billion-year half-life lets astronomers estimate the ages of old stars.
It is about three times as abundant as uranium in the crust and occurs mainly in monazite.
It is recovered as a byproduct of rare earth extraction from monazite sands, notably in India.
Jöns Jacob Berzelius discovered it in 1829 and named it after Thor, the Norse god of thunder.
uses: Thorium is being developed as a nuclear fuel, notably in India's long-term program and molten salt reactors.
Thoriated tungsten electrodes are used in TIG welding.
Thorium oxide has been used in high-temperature ceramics and high-quality camera lenses.
Historical: thorium oxide made gas lantern mantles glow brightly.

who: Frederick Soddy, John Cranston, Otto Hahn, Lise Meitner
origin: Greek: proto and actinium (parent of actinium); it forms actinium when it radioactively decays.
h: Protactinium's name means 'before actinium', because it decays into actinium.
f: Otto Hahn and Lise Meitner identified its longest-lived isotope, protactinium-231, in 1917–18.
It is one of the rarest and most expensive naturally occurring elements.
Being scarce, toxic and highly radioactive, it has no significant uses outside research.
Ratios of protactinium to thorium in ocean sediments help scientists study past ocean circulation.
from: Protactinium occurs in traces in uranium ores, produced by the decay of uranium-235 and uranium-238.
Its longest-lived isotope, protactinium-231, has a half-life of about 32,800 years.
Otto Hahn and Lise Meitner identified protactinium-231 in 1918.
In 1961 British chemists extracted about 125 grams from some 60 metric tons of uranium processing waste.
uses: Research only: comparing protactinium-231 with thorium-230 in ocean sediments reveals past ocean circulation.
Research only: protactinium-233 is a step in the thorium fuel cycle, decaying to fissile uranium-233.

origin: Named for the planet Uranus.
h: A uranium nucleus can split in two; that fission, discovered in 1938, powers nuclear reactors and atomic weapons.
f: Martin Heinrich Klaproth discovered it in 1789 and named it after the recently found planet Uranus.
Henri Becquerel discovered radioactivity in 1896 using uranium salts.
Natural uranium is over 99 percent uranium-238; most reactors need fuel enriched in uranium-235.
About two billion years ago, natural nuclear reactors ran on their own in uranium deposits at Oklo, Gabon.
from: Uranium is made by rapid neutron capture in neutron star mergers and possibly rare supernovae.
Its main ore is uraninite, also called pitchblende, and uranium is dissolved in small amounts in seawater.
Kazakhstan is the largest producer, followed by Canada, Namibia and Australia.
Much uranium is extracted by in-situ leaching and concentrated into a powder called yellowcake.
uses: Enriched uranium fuels nuclear power plants, which generate about a tenth of the world's electricity.
Highly enriched uranium powers naval reactors and is used in nuclear weapons.
Depleted uranium is used in armor-piercing ammunition, tank armor and aircraft counterweights.
Uranium-lead dating gives the ages of the oldest rocks and of Earth itself.
Historical: uranium oxides gave glass and ceramic glazes a yellow-green color.

who: E. M. McMillan, P. H. Abelson
origin: Named for the planet Neptune.
h: Neptunium was the first element heavier than uranium ever made, and is named after Neptune, the planet beyond Uranus.
f: Edwin McMillan and Philip Abelson produced it at Berkeley in 1940 by bombarding uranium with neutrons.
Tiny traces occur naturally in uranium ores, formed when uranium captures neutrons.
Neptunium-237 is a by-product of nuclear reactors and is used to make plutonium-238.
Its longest-lived isotope, neptunium-237, has a half-life of about two million years.
from: Tiny traces of neptunium form in uranium ores when uranium-238 captures neutrons.
Edwin McMillan and Philip Abelson first made it in 1940 at Berkeley by bombarding uranium with neutrons.
Kilogram quantities build up in spent nuclear fuel and can be separated during reprocessing.
uses: Neptunium-237 is irradiated in reactors to produce plutonium-238 for spacecraft power.
Research only: neptunium-237 is studied as a long-lived and mobile part of nuclear waste.

who: G. T. Seaborg, J. W. Kennedy, E. M. McMillan, A. C. Wahl
origin: Named for the planet Pluto.
h: Plutonium-238 gives off so much heat that it powers deep-space probes like Voyager and Mars rovers like Curiosity.
f: Glenn Seaborg's team first made it at Berkeley in 1940–41.
It was named after Pluto, continuing the planetary pattern of uranium and neptunium.
Plutonium-239 fueled the first nuclear test, Trinity, and the bomb dropped on Nagasaki in 1945.
The metal has six different solid forms at normal pressure, an unusually complex behavior.
from: Trace plutonium forms in uranium ores through neutron capture.
Glenn Seaborg's team first made it in 1940 at Berkeley by bombarding uranium-238 with deuterons.
Plutonium-239 builds up in reactors when uranium-238 absorbs neutrons, and many tons exist in spent fuel.
Reprocessing separates plutonium chemically from spent fuel.
uses: Plutonium-239 is the fissile core of most nuclear weapons.
Mixed oxide fuel recycles plutonium in some nuclear power reactors.
Plutonium-238 generators power deep-space probes and the Mars rovers Curiosity and Perseverance.
Historical: some early pacemakers ran on plutonium-238 batteries.

who: G. T. Seaborg, R. A. James, L. O. Morgan, A. Ghiorso
origin: Named for the American continent, by analogy with europium.
h: A tiny speck of americium-241 sits inside many household smoke detectors, ionizing air so smoke can be sensed.
f: Glenn Seaborg's team identified it in 1944 at the University of Chicago's wartime Metallurgical Laboratory.
It was named after the Americas, echoing europium directly above it in the periodic table.
It is made in nuclear reactors when plutonium absorbs neutrons.
Americium-241 has a half-life of about 432 years.
from: Americium is produced in reactors when plutonium absorbs neutrons and then decays.
Glenn Seaborg's team first identified it in 1944 at the University of Chicago's Metallurgical Laboratory.
Americium-241 builds up in stored plutonium from the decay of plutonium-241 and is separated chemically.
uses: Tiny amounts of americium-241 ionize the air in household smoke detectors.
Americium-beryllium sources supply neutrons for oil well logging and soil moisture gauges.
Americium-241 is being developed as a long-lived heat source for European space missions.

who: G. T. Seaborg, R. A. James, A. Ghiorso
origin: Named in honor of Pierre and Marie Curie.
h: Curium is named after Marie and Pierre Curie, pioneers in the study of radioactivity.
f: Seaborg, Ralph James and Albert Ghiorso first made it in 1944 by bombarding plutonium with alpha particles.
Seaborg revealed its discovery on a children's radio quiz show in 1945, before the official announcement.
Curium-244 sources power instruments that analyze rocks on several Mars rovers.
Its longest-lived isotope, curium-247, has a half-life of about 16 million years.
from: Curium is made in reactors by repeated neutron capture in plutonium and americium.
Glenn Seaborg, Ralph James and Albert Ghiorso first made it in 1944 by bombarding plutonium-239 with alpha particles.
It was named after Marie and Pierre Curie.
uses: Curium-244 provides the alpha particles in X-ray spectrometers on Mars rovers.
Curium-248 targets bombarded with calcium-48 were used to create livermorium.

who: G. T. Seaborg, S. G. Thompson, A. Ghiorso
origin: Named after Berkeley, California the city of its discovery.
h: Berkelium is named after Berkeley, California, where it was first made in 1949.
f: Stanley Thompson, Albert Ghiorso and Glenn Seaborg made it by bombarding americium with alpha particles.
Only tiny amounts have ever been produced, mostly at Oak Ridge National Laboratory.
Berkelium targets were used to create element 117, tennessine.
Its longest-lived isotope, berkelium-247, has a half-life of about 1,400 years.
from: Berkelium is made in high-flux reactors by long neutron irradiation of curium.
Stanley Thompson, Albert Ghiorso and Glenn Seaborg first made it in 1949 at Berkeley by bombarding americium-241 with alpha particles.
Only milligram amounts exist, mostly produced at Oak Ridge's High Flux Isotope Reactor.
uses: Berkelium-249 targets bombarded with calcium-48 created tennessine.
Research only: chemists study its compounds to understand how heavy actinides form bonds.

who: G. T. Seaborg, S. G. Thompson, A. Ghiorso, K. Street Jr.
origin: Named after the state and University of California.
h: Californium-252 gives off so many neutrons that tiny amounts are used to start nuclear reactors and probe rocks in oil wells.
f: It was first made at Berkeley in 1950 and named after the state of California.
It is one of the heaviest elements ever produced in weighable amounts.
Californium targets were used to create element 118, oganesson.
Its neutrons are also used to detect explosives and analyze materials.
from: Californium is made by prolonged neutron irradiation of curium and plutonium in high-flux reactors.
It was first made in 1950 at Berkeley by bombarding curium-242 with alpha particles.
Oak Ridge's High Flux Isotope Reactor produces most of the world's small supply.
uses: Californium-252 is an intense neutron source used to start up nuclear reactors.
Its neutrons are used in oil well logging, moisture gauges and scanners that detect explosives.
Californium-249 targets bombarded with calcium-48 produced oganesson.

who: Argonne, Los Alamos and UC Berkeley
origin: Named in honor of the scientist Albert Einstein.
h: Einsteinium was first found in debris from the first full-scale hydrogen bomb test, 'Ivy Mike', in 1952.
f: Its discovery was kept secret for several years because of Cold War security.
It is named after Albert Einstein.
Only tiny amounts have ever been made, usually well under a milligram at a time.
In 2021, researchers measured some of its chemistry using a sample of only a few hundred nanograms.
from: Einsteinium was discovered in debris from Ivy Mike, the first hydrogen bomb test, in 1952.
In the blast, uranium captured many neutrons almost instantly, briefly mimicking the rapid neutron-capture process.
It is now made in tiny amounts in high-flux reactors by irradiating lighter actinides.
It was named after Albert Einstein.
uses: Research only: einsteinium-253 targets were used in 1955 to make the first atoms of mendelevium.
Research only: microgram samples let scientists measure basic chemical properties such as its bond lengths.

who: Argonne, Los Alamos and UC Berkeley
origin: Named in honor of the scientist Enrico Fermi.
h: Fermium is the heaviest element that can be built up by bombarding lighter elements with neutrons.
f: It was first identified, alongside einsteinium, in debris from the 1952 'Ivy Mike' hydrogen bomb test.
It is named after Enrico Fermi, who led the team that built the first nuclear reactor.
No visible amount of fermium has ever been made, so its bulk properties are only predicted.
Its longest-lived isotope, fermium-257, has a half-life of about 100 days.
from: Fermium was found alongside einsteinium in the debris of the 1952 Ivy Mike test.
It is the heaviest element that can be made by neutron capture in reactors, and only in tiny amounts.
Fermium-258 fissions spontaneously in a fraction of a millisecond, blocking further neutron capture.
It was named after Enrico Fermi.
uses: Research only: its isotopes help physicists understand how very heavy nuclei split.

who: A. Ghiorso, B. G. Harvey, G. R. Choppin, S. G. Thompson, G. T. Seaborg
origin: Named in honor of the scientist Dmitri Ivanovitch Mendeleyev, who devised the periodic table.
h: Mendelevium was first made in 1955 literally one atom at a time: just 17 atoms in the original experiments.
f: It is named after Dmitri Mendeleev, creator of the periodic table.
Albert Ghiorso, Glenn Seaborg and colleagues made it at Berkeley by bombarding einsteinium with alpha particles.
Its longest-lived known isotope, mendelevium-258, has a half-life of about 51 days.
Its bulk properties have never been measured; most are predictions.
from: Mendelevium was first made in 1955 at Berkeley by bombarding einsteinium-253 with alpha particles.
The discovery experiments detected only 17 atoms.
It is still made in accelerators a few atoms at a time.
It is named after Dmitri Mendeleev, creator of the periodic table.
uses: Research only: chemists probe its chemistry one atom at a time, including its +2 oxidation state.

origin: Named in honor of Alfred Nobel, who invented dynamite and founded Nobel prize.
h: Nobelium is named after Alfred Nobel, but its discovery was hotly disputed by laboratories in Sweden, the US and the USSR.
f: The name came from a 1957 claim made in Stockholm that later proved to be wrong.
Scientists at Dubna, in the USSR, were eventually credited with the first reliable synthesis in the 1960s.
Its longest-lived known isotope has a half-life of just under an hour.
It can only be made a few atoms at a time, so its chemistry is studied atom by atom.
from: Nobelium's discovery was disputed for years; Soviet scientists at Dubna are credited with conclusive work in the 1960s.
It is commonly made today by bombarding lead-208 with calcium-48 ions.
It is named after Alfred Nobel.
uses: Research only: laser spectroscopy of single nobelium atoms tests theories of how electrons behave in heavy atoms.

who: A. Ghiorso, T. Sikkeland, A. E. Larsh, R. M. Latimer
origin: Named in honor of Ernest O. Lawrence, inventor of the cyclotron.
h: Lawrencium, named after cyclotron inventor Ernest Lawrence, is the last member of the actinide series.
f: Albert Ghiorso's team at Berkeley first reported it in 1961 by bombarding californium with boron.
Credit for its discovery was eventually shared between teams at Berkeley and Dubna.
Its longest-lived known isotope has a half-life of about 11 hours.
In 2015, researchers measured its ionization energy using one atom at a time.
from: Lawrencium was first reported in 1961 at Berkeley by bombarding californium with boron ions.
It is made atom by atom in accelerators.
It is named after Ernest Lawrence, inventor of the cyclotron.
uses: Research only: measuring its ionization energy in 2015 helped settle debates about its place in the periodic table.

origin: Named in honor of Ernest Rutherford
h: Rutherfordium, the first element beyond the actinides, is named after Ernest Rutherford, a founding father of nuclear physics.
f: Soviet and American teams both claimed it, in 1964 and 1969, and proposed different names.
Its name was settled by IUPAC in 1997, after decades of dispute.
Even its longest-lived known isotopes decay within hours.
Experiments on single atoms suggest it behaves like hafnium, the element above it.
from: Rutherfordium was claimed by Dubna in 1964 and by Berkeley in 1969, which bombarded californium-249 with carbon-12.
It is made atom by atom by fusing heavy targets with beams of lighter ions.
It is named after Ernest Rutherford.
uses: Research only: single-atom chemistry experiments show it behaves much like hafnium and zirconium.

origin: Named after the city of Dubna, the site of the JINR.
h: Dubnium is named after Dubna, the Russian science town where much of the hunt for superheavy elements has taken place.
f: It was reported by Dubna in 1968 and by Berkeley in 1970, sparking a long naming dispute.
That rivalry over element names became known as the 'Transfermium Wars'.
Even its longest-lived known isotopes decay within about a day.
Single-atom chemistry suggests it resembles niobium and tantalum, but its bulk properties are unknown.
from: Dubnium was made between 1968 and 1970 at Dubna and Berkeley, using americium and californium targets.
Its longest-lived isotopes last for hours, unusually long for a superheavy element.
It is named after Dubna, Russia, home of the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research.
uses: Research only: chemists compare it with niobium and tantalum to test how relativity alters chemistry.

who: Joint Institute for Nuclear Research and UC Berkeley
origin: Named in honor of Glenn Seaborg, American physical chemist known for research on transuranium elements.
h: Seaborgium was the first element named after a person who was still alive: American chemist Glenn T. Seaborg.
f: It was first made at Berkeley in 1974 by bombarding californium with oxygen ions.
Seaborg helped discover ten elements and shared the 1951 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
Its known isotopes last from fractions of a second to several minutes.
Single-atom experiments suggest it behaves like tungsten, the element above it.
from: Seaborgium was first made in 1974 at Berkeley by bombarding californium-249 with oxygen-18.
Only a few atoms are made at a time in accelerators.
It is named after Glenn Seaborg, who was alive when the name was chosen.
uses: Research only: experiments show seaborgium forms compounds similar to those of tungsten.

who: GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research
origin: Named in honor of Niels Bohr
h: Bohrium is named after Niels Bohr, whose model of the atom helped launch quantum physics.
f: A team at the GSI laboratory in Darmstadt, Germany, first convincingly made it in 1981.
Only a few atoms are made at a time, each decaying within seconds to minutes.
Chemistry experiments on a handful of atoms showed it behaves like rhenium, the element above it.
Its bulk properties have never been measured and are only predicted.
from: Bohrium was first made in 1981 at GSI in Darmstadt, Germany, by bombarding bismuth-209 with chromium-54.
Only small numbers of atoms have ever been made.
It is named after Niels Bohr.
uses: Research only: gas-phase studies of bohrium oxychloride show it behaves like rhenium.

who: GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research
origin: Named in honor of Henri Hess, Swiss born Russian chemist known for work in thermodydamics.
h: Hassium is named after the German state of Hesse, home of the GSI laboratory where it was first made in 1984.
f: It was made by fusing iron nuclei with lead.
In 2001, single-atom experiments showed it forms a volatile oxide, just like osmium above it.
Only small numbers of its very short-lived atoms have ever been made.
As a metal it is predicted to be extremely dense, but no bulk sample has ever existed.
from: Hassium was first made in 1984 at GSI by bombarding lead-208 with iron-58.
It is produced only a few atoms at a time.
It is named after the German state of Hesse, home of GSI.
uses: Research only: experiments in 2001 made hassium tetroxide, confirming it as a heavier relative of osmium.

who: GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research
origin: Named in honor of Lise Mietner
h: Meitnerium honors Lise Meitner, who helped explain nuclear fission but was left out of the Nobel Prize for it.
f: A team at GSI in Darmstadt first detected a single atom of it in 1982.
It was made by bombarding bismuth with iron nuclei.
Its known isotopes decay within seconds.
Its chemistry has never been studied; it is predicted to resemble iridium.
from: Meitnerium was first made in 1982 at GSI by bombarding bismuth-209 with iron-58, yielding a single atom.
Few atoms have been made since, and its chemistry has never been studied.
It is named after Lise Meitner, who helped explain nuclear fission.
uses: Research only: its short-lived isotopes help map the stability of superheavy nuclei.

who: GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research
origin: Named after the city of Darmstadt, Germany where  GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research is located.
h: Darmstadtium is named after Darmstadt, Germany, where GSI scientists first made it in 1994.
f: It was made by fusing nickel nuclei with lead.
Only a small number of atoms have ever been detected, each lasting seconds at most.
It is predicted to be a dense metal resembling platinum, but this has never been tested.
Its name was officially approved in 2003.
from: Darmstadtium was first made in 1994 at GSI by bombarding lead-208 with nickel-62.
Its known isotopes decay within seconds or less.
It is named after Darmstadt, the German city where GSI is located.
uses: Research only: physicists study its decay chains to understand the structure of superheavy nuclei.

who: GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research
origin: Named in honor of the physicist Wilhelm Roentgen.
h: Roentgenium is named after Wilhelm Röntgen, who discovered X-rays in 1895.
f: GSI scientists first made three atoms of it in 1994 by fusing nickel and bismuth.
It sits below gold and is predicted to be a noble metal, but its chemistry is untested.
Its known isotopes decay within minutes at most.
Its name was officially approved in 2004.
from: Roentgenium was first made in 1994 at GSI by bombarding bismuth-209 with nickel-64.
Heavier, longer-lived isotopes appear in the decay chains of elements made at Dubna.
It is named after Wilhelm Röntgen, discoverer of X-rays.
uses: Research only: theory predicts a gold-like metal whose properties are strongly shaped by relativity.

who: GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research
origin: Named in honor of the astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus.
h: Copernicium, named after astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus, behaves in single-atom experiments like a volatile relative of mercury.
f: GSI scientists first made it in 1996 by fusing zinc and lead nuclei.
Its name was announced on February 19, 2010, Copernicus's birthday.
Some calculations predict it may be liquid near room temperature, but this has never been measured.
Its longest-lived known isotope lasts about half a minute.
from: Copernicium was first made in 1996 at GSI by bombarding lead-208 with zinc-70.
Heavier isotopes made through calcium-48 reactions last up to about half a minute.
It is named after Nicolaus Copernicus.
uses: Research only: one-atom chemistry suggests it is a very volatile metal, possibly liquid near room temperature.

origin: Named after the country of Japan.
h: Nihonium was the first element discovered in Asia; Japan's RIKEN team spent nine years collecting just three atoms.
f: Its name comes from 'Nihon', one of the Japanese names for Japan.
RIKEN made it by fusing zinc and bismuth nuclei.
A Russian–American team also reported it, but IUPAC credited RIKEN in 2015.
Its isotopes decay within seconds, and its chemistry is largely predicted.
from: Nihonium was first created at RIKEN in Japan by bombarding bismuth-209 with zinc-70, starting in 2003.
RIKEN detected only three atoms over nine years of experiments.
Dubna also observed it as a decay product of moscovium.
It is named after Nihon, a Japanese name for Japan, and is the first element discovered in Asia.
uses: Research only: chemists are beginning to compare its behavior with thallium, its lighter relative.

origin: Named after the Flerov Laboratory of Nuclear Reactions of the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research in Dubna, Russia.
h: Flerovium was first made at Dubna, Russia, in 1998, and honors physicist Georgy Flyorov, founder of its laboratory.
f: It was made by fusing calcium-48 with plutonium.
Its isotopes live up to a few seconds, intriguing scientists searching for a predicted 'island of stability'.
Single-atom experiments suggest it is fairly volatile, but its chemistry is still debated.
IUPAC approved its name in 2012, alongside livermorium.
from: Flerovium was first made around 1999 at Dubna by bombarding plutonium-244 with calcium-48.
Its isotopes lie near the predicted island of stability and last up to a few seconds.
It is named after the Flerov Laboratory of Nuclear Reactions, which honors Georgy Flerov.
uses: Research only: experiments test whether it behaves like a volatile metal or nearly like a noble gas.

origin: Named after the city of Moscov.
h: Moscovium is named after the Moscow region, home of Dubna, where it was first made in 2003.
f: A Russian–American team made it by firing calcium-48 nuclei at americium.
Its isotopes decay in under a second.
Its chemistry and bulk properties are almost entirely predicted, not measured.
IUPAC confirmed its discovery in 2015 and approved the name in 2016.
from: Moscovium was first reported in 2004 by Dubna and Livermore, bombarding americium-243 with calcium-48.
Each atom lasts well under a second before undergoing alpha decay.
It is named after the Moscow region, home of Dubna.
uses: Research only: moscovium decay chains helped confirm the discovery of nihonium.

origin: Named after the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in the United States.
h: Livermorium honors Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in California, whose scientists helped a Russian team make it.
f: It was first made at Dubna in 2000 by fusing calcium-48 with curium.
Its isotopes decay within a fraction of a second.
It sits below polonium in the periodic table, but its properties are only predicted.
IUPAC approved its name in 2012, alongside flerovium.
from: Livermorium was first made in 2000 at Dubna by bombarding curium-248 with calcium-48.
It is named after Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, which collaborated with Dubna.
In 2024 Berkeley made it with a titanium-50 beam, a step toward creating element 120.
uses: Research only: its isotopes help map nuclear stability near the island of stability.

who: Joint Institute for Nuclear Research and Oak Ridge National Laboratory
origin: Named after the state of Tennessee in United States.
h: Making tennessine required rare berkelium from a Tennessee reactor, flown to Russia and bombarded with calcium ions.
f: A Russian–American collaboration first reported it in 2010.
It is named after Tennessee, home of Oak Ridge National Laboratory and other partner institutions.
It sits among the halogens, but is predicted to be far more metal-like than fluorine or chlorine.
Its known isotopes decay within tens of milliseconds.
from: Tennessine was first made in 2010 at Dubna by bombarding berkelium-249 with calcium-48.
The rare berkelium target was produced at Oak Ridge National Laboratory's High Flux Isotope Reactor in Tennessee.
It is named after Tennessee, home of Oak Ridge, Vanderbilt University and the University of Tennessee.
uses: Research only: its decay chains extend knowledge of the heaviest isotopes and test predictions of nuclear stability.

origin: Named in honor of the scientist Yuri Oganessian.
h: Oganesson, element 118, completes the periodic table's seventh row, and only a handful of its atoms have ever been detected.
f: It is only the second element named after a living person, nuclear physicist Yuri Oganessian.
It was made at Dubna, starting in 2002, by firing calcium-48 nuclei at californium.
Its known isotope decays in under a millisecond.
Though grouped with the noble gases, it is predicted to be a solid and possibly fairly reactive.
from: Oganesson was first made at Dubna in 2002 and 2005 by bombarding californium-249 with calcium-48 ions.
Only a handful of atoms have been detected, each decaying in under a millisecond.
It is named after physicist Yuri Oganessian, one of only two people honored by an element while alive.
It is the heaviest known element and sits at the bottom of the noble gas column.
uses: Research only: theory predicts relativistic effects make it a reactive solid, unlike the other noble gases.
Research only: it completes the seventh row of the periodic table, and searches for elements 119 and 120 continue.
